units.title: Basics: jobs and Burst
units.blurb: Two separate things — threads and a compiler, what Burst can and cannot compile, the kinds of jobs and Schedule versus Run versus Complete. This is where they check you have really used them.

lessons.title: Two separate things
lessons.sub: The Job System is threads, Burst is a compiler. People mix them up, and interviewers know it

cards.title: The Job System and Burst are not the same thing
cards.body:
A performance interview often opens with an easy one: “How is the Job System different from Burst?” The right answer: they are two independent things that work well together.

The Job System is about threads. You describe work as a job struct, and the engine spreads it over worker threads, respects the dependencies between jobs and, in the Editor, catches data races through the safety system.

Burst is about compilation. It is a compiler: it takes the IL of your C# and, through LLVM, turns it into native machine code for a specific CPU — with SIMD vector instructions that process 4–8 numbers in one operation. It does not compile all of C#, only a subset called HPC# (High-Performance C#): structs, primitives, native containers, no managed objects.

In short: the Job System answers “on which threads”, Burst answers “with what machine code”.

cards.title: What a job looks like
cards.body:
A job is a struct that implements a job interface; the simplest is IJob with a single Execute() method. The struct’s fields are its input and output.

The job gets a copy of the struct, so results come back only through a native container such as NativeArray<T>: its copy points at the same unmanaged memory. Fields cannot hold references to managed objects, and main-thread APIs (Time, transform, Physics) are not available inside a job — you pass what you need in fields, for example dt = Time.deltaTime. The [ReadOnly] attribute says the job only reads a field.

Schedule() queues the job and returns a JobHandle; Complete() waits for it to finish — only then may the main thread read the result.

A native container is allocated with an allocator and freed by hand with Dispose(): Allocator.TempJob lives a few frames, for a job; Allocator.Persistent lives long, for example for the lifetime of a component. Data and allocators are covered in unit 2, Schedule and Complete in lesson 4.

cards.q: What does Burst do?
options: Compiles a subset of C# (HPC#) through LLVM into native code with SIMD instructions
Spreads jobs over the worker threads
Looks for data races between jobs
Speeds up any C# code, classes and LINQ included
cards.explain: Burst is a compiler, not a scheduler. It takes IL, hands it to LLVM and gets machine code for the target CPU. Threads, the queue and race checks come from the Job System.

wrong.1: That is the Job System’s job: threads, the queue, dependencies. Burst knows nothing about threads.
wrong.2: Races are caught by the Job System’s safety system — and only in the Editor.
wrong.3: Burst compiles only HPC#: structs, primitives, native containers. Classes and LINQ are managed objects; it will not take them.

cards.title: Four combinations
cards.body:
Since they are independent, there are four ways to combine them:

1. Plain C# on the main thread. The starting point: Mono or IL2CPP, one thread.

2. A job without Burst. The work moves to worker threads, but inside it is the same managed code. You gain parallelism, not better code.

3. Burst without worker threads. [BurstCompile] on a static method called from the main thread, or job.Run() — a Burst job executed right away on the current thread, with no queue. No extra threads, but the hot code is now native.

4. Job + Burst. Parallel and native — the usual choice for heavy loops.

Interviewers like it when you know about the third option: not every task is worth splitting across threads, but almost every hot numeric loop gains from Burst.

cards.title: [BurstCompile] on a static method
cards.body:
Burst compiles not only jobs but also static methods that you call directly from ordinary code. The rules are stricter than people expect:

— [BurstCompile] goes on the method and on the type that declares it;
— the method is static and not generic, and its declaring type is not generic either;
— parameters are primitives, pointers and structs only by ref, in or pointer: you cannot pass a struct by value, and results come back through out;
— most native containers, NativeArray included, cannot cross this boundary: they carry managed safety-system fields. You pass an array as a pointer and a length.

Under the hood a direct call becomes a call through a function pointer, and the transition has a cost: for a tiny method it can eat the gain. It pays to hand such a method a whole batch of work at once.

cards.q: You want to call a Burst method directly from the main thread. What does that require? Pick all that apply.
options: [BurstCompile] on both the method and the class that declares it
The method is static and not generic
Structs are passed by ref, in or pointer
The method is started with Schedule()
A NativeArray is passed as a by-value parameter
cards.explain: A direct Burst call has nothing to do with jobs: no Schedule(), same thread. The attribute goes on the method and on the type, generics are not supported, structs go only by reference or pointer, and a NativeArray cannot cross the boundary because of its safety-system fields — you pass a pointer and a length.

cards.title: Where the speed-up comes from
cards.body:
Burst beats ordinary C# for several reasons at once:

— SIMD: a loop over a float array compiles to instructions that handle 4 (SSE, NEON) or 8 (AVX) numbers at a time;
— LLVM: aggressive optimizations — inlining, loop unrolling, hoisting invariants;
— code for the specific CPU and with no managed plumbing: no GC and no objects in the hot loop;
— data sits densely in native containers, so there are fewer cache misses.

You can see the result in the Burst Inspector (Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector): it shows the assembly of every job.

On number crunching — loops over arrays of numbers and vectors — the gain is usually several times, and on well-vectorized code it can be an order of magnitude. But at the interview quote your own number, measured: “Profile first, then Burst the hot loop.” If the bottleneck is not computation but, say, GameObject work, Burst will not help.
cards.deep: In the Editor Burst compiles asynchronously: until compilation finishes, the job runs as ordinary managed code. For measurements in the Editor turn on Jobs > Burst > Synchronous Compilation or use [BurstCompile(CompileSynchronously = true)], and let the code warm up. In a player build the code is always compiled ahead of time (AOT), so the setting does not exist there.

cards.q: A job is scheduled with Schedule() but has no [BurstCompile]. What do you get?
options: Parallelism on worker threads, but inside it is ordinary managed code without Burst optimizations
A compile error: a job must use Burst
The same native code: Burst turns itself on for every job
The job runs on the main thread
cards.explain: The Job System works without Burst — that is combination 2. You get the speed-up from threads but not from the compiler. In production, jobs are usually marked [BurstCompile] whenever the code fits HPC#.

wrong.1: The Job System does not need Burst: a job without the attribute is ordinary managed code on a worker thread.
wrong.2: Burst is switched on only by the [BurstCompile] attribute.
wrong.3: Schedule() hands the job to the scheduler, and it is normally the worker threads that run it. Run() is what executes a job right away on the current thread.

cards.task: Move the loop from Update into a job: struct MoveJob : IJob with [BurstCompile], fields positions, velocities (with [ReadOnly]) and float dt. In Update create the job, pass Time.deltaTime into dt, call Schedule() and then Complete() (right after each other for now — lesson 4 spreads them across the frame). No loop should remain in Update.

checks.label: MoveJob is an IJob struct with the [BurstCompile] attribute
velocities is marked [ReadOnly]
MoveJob has a public float dt field
Execute() changes positions[i]
Update calls Schedule() and then Complete()
There is no for loop in Update

cards.explain: The loop body moved into Execute(), the data into the job’s fields. Time.deltaTime is read on the main thread and passed by value, because Unity APIs are not available in a job. [ReadOnly] on velocities says the job never changes that array. At the interview you put it the same way: data into native containers, the loop into Execute, the job under Burst, and Complete() as late as possible.

cards.q: Interviewer: “Why Burst, if you can just spread the work over threads?” Which answer is stronger?
options: Threads split the work across cores, while Burst speeds up the code itself on each core — SIMD and LLVM optimizations. The effects add up
Burst is not needed once the jobs are parallel
Burst only matters on mobile devices
Jobs do not work in a player build without Burst
cards.explain: On 8 cores threads give at most ~8x, and only with a perfect split. Burst speeds up every iteration. That is why a heavy loop usually gets combination 4 — a job plus Burst — and the numbers come from the profiler.

wrong.1: Parallelism and code quality are independent axes: parallel managed code is still scalar and still carries managed plumbing.
wrong.2: Burst generates code for x86 and ARM; the gain on desktop is just as real.
wrong.3: A job without Burst works everywhere — it is ordinary managed code on a worker thread.

cards.q: Put the steps in order: moving a hot loop to Jobs + Burst.
items: Find the hot loop in the profiler
Move the data into a NativeArray
Move the loop body into Execute() of a job struct
Mark the job [BurstCompile]
Measure again and compare with the original
cards.explain: Measure first, or you may speed up the wrong thing. Then data into native containers, the loop into a job, Burst — and measure again: “Profile first, then Burst the hot loop.”

lessons.title: What Burst can and cannot compile
lessons.sub: HPC# without managed objects, strings in Debug.Log, and why throw crashes a player build

cards.title: HPC#: C# without managed objects
cards.body:
Burst generates native code that has no garbage collector and no .NET runtime. Hence the main rule of HPC#: no managed objects — nothing that lives on the managed heap.

Not allowed:
— classes and any reference types, List<T> and Dictionary included;
— managed arrays T[] (the exception is a static readonly array that you only read directly: Burst copies it at compile time);
— strings as values, string methods, char and decimal;
— delegates and lambdas;
— boxing: casting a struct to object or to an interface creates a heap object;
— virtual calls — they need a class instance;
— catch (while try/finally and using do work);
— writes to ordinary static fields.

Burst reports such code as a compile error in the console, pointing at the line.

cards.title: What to use instead
cards.body:
Every ban has a Burst-friendly replacement:

— structs instead of classes;
— native containers instead of arrays and collections: NativeArray<T>, NativeList<T>, NativeHashMap and the rest of the Collections package;
— Unity.Mathematics — float3, float4x4, the math.* functions: Burst knows these types and vectorizes them well;
— pointers and unsafe code, stackalloc for a small scratch buffer on the stack;
— FixedString32Bytes, FixedString64Bytes, FixedString128Bytes — a fixed-capacity string stored right inside the struct;
— FunctionPointer<T> instead of a delegate;
— SharedStatic<T> instead of a mutable static field.

System.Math, Interlocked and try/finally also work.

cards.q: Match the managed code with its Burst replacement.

cards.title: Strings and Debug.Log
cards.body:
Burst has no strings as values, but two string features do work — and interviewers like to ask about them.

Debug.Log, Debug.LogWarning and Debug.LogError accept a string literal or an interpolated $"..." (and string.Format) with a literal template. Arguments may only be built-in value types (int, float, bool…) and Unity.Mathematics vectors. Burst builds the message itself, with no managed string.

A literal or the same kind of interpolation can be assigned to a FixedString. What you cannot do is pass a string to your own method, keep it in a struct field, concatenate with + or call ToString() — those are methods of a managed object.

cards.q: Which of these will Burst compile? Pick all that apply.
options: Debug.Log($"count = {count}") with an int count
try/finally around work with a buffer
A static readonly int[] table that is only read directly
catch (Exception e) { … }
A string name field in a job struct
object o = myStruct;
cards.explain: Interpolation with a primitive in Debug.Log is supported, so is try/finally, and Burst copies a static readonly array at compile time. catch is not supported, a string field is a managed object, and object o = myStruct is boxing, which means a heap object.

cards.task: Make DamageJob Burst-compatible: damage becomes NativeArray<float>, crits becomes NativeArray<int> (both are only read, so mark them [ReadOnly]), and the log uses $"..." interpolation with the number instead of string concatenation and ToString().

checks.label: damage is a [ReadOnly] NativeArray<float>
crits is a [ReadOnly] NativeArray<int>
No managed T[] arrays and no List<T>
Debug.Log gets a $"..." interpolation
No ToString() and no string concatenation with +

cards.explain: The managed collections became native containers, so the data now sits in unmanaged memory that Burst can see. Count turned into Length. Burst builds the message from the literal template and the number itself — no managed string appears. At the interview: “Burst has no managed objects: NativeArray and NativeList instead of T[] and List, FixedString instead of string, and logs are a literal or $"" with primitives.”

cards.title: What throw does
cards.body:
Burst supports throw only in a simple form — throw new ArgumentException("literal"): the message is embedded in the code statically. What happens next depends on where the code runs:

— in the Editor the exception is forwarded to managed code and printed to the console — it looks like ordinary C#;
— in a player build a throw from Burst code aborts the application. Compiler warning BC1370 tells you exactly that.

That is why checks that throw go into a method marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")]. The symbol is defined in the Editor and not in player builds, so neither the method nor its calls make it into the build. The native containers’ own checks work this way: a clear error in the Editor, zero cost in the build. Safety checks are simply unavailable in player builds, not “off by default”.
cards.deep: Two subtleties. If an exception does happen, Burst behaves as if there were no finally blocks — do not rely on finally to release resources on an exception. And if a file has both using UnityEngine; and using System.Diagnostics;, the name Debug becomes ambiguous; then write the attribute in full: [System.Diagnostics.Conditional(...)].

cards.q: A Burst job throws ArgumentException when an index is out of range. What does the player see in a release build when that happens?
options: The application aborts: a throw in Burst code in a player build is an abort
An exception in the log, and the game carries on
Nothing: the build silently skips the throw
The job restarts on the main thread
cards.explain: In a player build nothing can catch an exception from Burst code, so the app goes down. To get a clear error in the Editor without crashing the build, put the throwing check in a method marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")].

wrong.1: That is the Editor’s behaviour: there the exception is forwarded to managed code. A player build has no such path.
wrong.2: Only checks inside [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")] methods vanish from the build, together with the method. An ordinary throw stays and crashes the app.
wrong.3: No such mechanism exists.

cards.task: In FillJob the count check throws right inside Execute — in a player build that crashes the app. Move the check into static void CheckCount(int count, int length) marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")] and call it from Execute. Keep the message a string literal.

checks.label: System.Diagnostics is imported (or the attribute is written in full)
CheckCount is marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")]
The throw is inside CheckCount
Execute calls CheckCount
There is no throw in Execute

cards.explain: In the Editor the check runs and gives a clear exception in the console. In a player build ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS is not defined, so the compiler drops both the method and the call — the throw never reaches native code. The bounds checks inside NativeArray and NativeList work the same way.

cards.title: Without virtual calls or boxing
cards.body:
Polymorphism through classes is not available in Burst, but there are two honest ways around it.

Generics with a struct constraint. If the job is generic over T : struct, IRule, Burst knows the concrete type and calls the method directly: no boxing, no virtual call, and the method can be inlined. The price is a separate copy of the code for each concrete T, and the choice is made at scheduling time, not in the middle of the loop.

FunctionPointer<T> — a pointer to a Burst-compiled static method: the behaviour is chosen at run time. The price is an indirect call that blocks inlining and vectorization (more in unit 3).

But IRule rule = new DoubleRule(); is boxing: the struct is wrapped in a heap object, and Burst code cannot do that.

And the simplest option, which people forget: a switch on an enum field inside a single job.

cards.q: Which line will not compile under Burst?
cards.explain: object boxed = sum is boxing: the int is wrapped in an object on the managed heap. foreach over a NativeArray is supported, and a FixedString32Bytes field is a fine replacement for a string.

cards.q: Interviewer: “A Burst job has to apply one of three behaviour rules. How would you do it?”
options: A generic job with T : struct, IRule when the rule is known at scheduling time; FunctionPointer<T> when it has to be chosen at run time
An abstract Rule class with a virtual Apply method
A Func<float, float> field in the job struct
A field of type IRule holding the rule struct
cards.explain: A generic over a struct gives a direct call with no boxing — the fastest option. FunctionPointer<T> covers the case where the type is not known in advance, at the cost of an indirect call. Another simple route is a switch on an enum inside one job.

wrong.1: A class is a managed object, and a virtual call needs an object.
wrong.2: A delegate is a managed object; its Burst replacement is FunctionPointer<T>.
wrong.3: A struct stored in an interface-typed field is boxing.

lessons.title: Kinds of jobs
lessons.sub: IJob, IJobParallelFor, IJobFor, transforms and Entities jobs — which to pick and why

cards.title: IJob: one task on one thread
cards.body:
There are several job types, and “which one would you pick” shows whether you understand how work is split between threads.

IJob has one Execute() method that runs entirely on a single worker thread. It runs in parallel only with the main thread and with other jobs; the work itself is not split.

It fits work that does not cut into independent pieces: sorting, a sum, building a data structure, a step that depends on the previous result.

cards.title: IJobParallelFor: Execute for every index
cards.body:
IJobParallelFor calls Execute(int index) for every index from 0 up to the given length. When scheduling you pass the length and the batch size — the innerloopBatchCount parameter, usually called batchSize: that is how many iterations a worker grabs at a time. The workers take batches, and an idle worker steals batches from busy ones (work stealing). That is why the order of iterations is not guaranteed.

The safety rule: in Execute(index) you write only to element [index]. In the Editor the safety system stops a write to someone else’s index with an exception — that is how it guards against races between batches.

For light per-element work batchSize is usually 32–128, for very heavy work it can go down to 1. Details are in unit 2, and the profiler always has the last word.

cards.q: An IJobParallelFor over 10,000 elements with batchSize 64. What is true?
options: Iterations run in batches of 64 on different worker threads, and the order of batches is not guaranteed
Execute is called 64 times
Iterations run strictly in order from 0 to 9999
Each iteration runs on its own thread
cards.explain: Execute is called 10,000 times — once per index. Workers grab 64 iterations at a time and steal batches from each other, so the order between batches is undefined. Hence the rule: every iteration is independent and writes only to its own index.

wrong.1: 64 is the batch size, not the number of calls. Execute is called for every index.
wrong.2: There is an order only inside one batch on one thread, not between batches.
wrong.3: There are as many threads as the Job System has workers, not as many as there are iterations.

cards.title: IJobFor: one job, three ways to run it
cards.body:
IJobFor (since Unity 2019.3) looks like IJobParallelFor — the same Execute(int index) — but how it runs is decided at the call site:

— Run(length) — right away, on the main thread, in order;
— Schedule(length, dependsOn) — on one worker thread, in order;
— ScheduleParallel(length, batchSize, dependsOn) — in batches on several worker threads, like IJobParallelFor.

dependsOn is the JobHandle of a job that must finish first; default means no dependencies. It is convenient: one struct, and you switch the mode with one line — Run for debugging, Schedule when the data is small or order matters, ScheduleParallel for big arrays.

The trap: Schedule on an IJobFor is not parallel.

cards.q: Match the call with where the work runs.
pairs: One whole Execute() on a worker thread
Right away on the main thread, in order
Execute(i) for every i on one worker thread
Batches of 64 on several worker threads

cards.title: IJobParallelForTransform: transforms from a job
cards.body:
A job cannot touch GameObject or Transform — they are managed main-thread objects. Transforms get an exception: a TransformAccessArray holds a list of transforms, and an IJobParallelForTransform gets access to position, rotation and scale in Execute(int index, TransformAccess transform).

An important detail: Schedule(transforms) gives read and write access but parallelizes only separate hierarchies — transforms with a shared root are always processed on the same thread. A thousand bullets under one container object is effectively one thread. Keep such objects at the scene root.

If you only need to read, there is ScheduleReadOnly(transforms, batchSize) (since 2020.2): it reads all transforms in parallel, whatever the hierarchy; check invalid entries with transform.isValid. A transform job has no plain Run — only RunReadOnly. Like native containers, a TransformAccessArray is freed with Dispose().

cards.q: What is true about IJobParallelForTransform? Pick all that apply.
options: With Schedule, transforms that share a root are processed on one thread
ScheduleReadOnly reads transforms in parallel regardless of the hierarchy
In Execute you can call GetComponent<Rigidbody>() on the transform
With Schedule, a thousand objects under one parent spread over all cores
A transform job has RunReadOnly but no plain Run
cards.explain: The read-write Schedule parallelizes only separate roots, so objects under one parent run on one thread. ScheduleReadOnly lifts that limit for reading. TransformAccess gives you position, rotation, scale and matrices, not the GameObject: there are no components inside a job.

cards.task: Rewrite DistanceJob from IJob to IJobParallelFor: Execute(int index) computes one distance and writes only to distances[index], with no loop inside. In ScheduleDistances schedule it with Schedule(positions.Length, 64).

checks.label: DistanceJob is an IJobParallelFor struct with [BurstCompile]
Execute takes an int index
Execute writes to distances at its own index
There is no for loop in Execute
Schedule gets the array length and a batchSize

cards.explain: The loop is gone: the scheduler took over its role, calling Execute for every index and handing batches of 64 to the worker threads. Each iteration is independent and writes only to its own element, so the safety system is happy and there are no races. For work this light per element, 64 is a reasonable starting batch.

cards.title: Other kinds: Collections and Entities
cards.body:
The Collections package adds specialised types: IJobParallelForDefer — when the length is unknown at scheduling time (for example, it is the length of a NativeList that an earlier job fills); IJobParallelForBatch — Execute(startIndex, count) receives a whole batch; IJobFilter — selecting indices.

Entities 1.x has jobs of its own. IJobEntity: you write an Execute whose parameters are components (ref to write, in to read), and the source generator turns it into a pass over every matching entity; the struct must be partial. IJobChunk is a level lower: Execute is called per chunk, and you fetch the component arrays yourself. You pick it when you need full control over how a chunk is walked. More in unit 4.

cards.q: Interviewer: “10,000 bullets are GameObjects, and each has to move every frame. Which job do you use?”
options: IJobParallelForTransform with a TransformAccessArray, keeping the bullets at the scene root rather than under one parent
IJobParallelFor that accesses a Transform[] array inside
An IJob that moves all bullets in a loop
IJobFor with Schedule — it is parallel
cards.explain: Transforms are touched from a job only through TransformAccessArray and IJobParallelForTransform. If all bullets sit under one parent, the read-write Schedule runs them on one thread — that is why the hierarchy is kept flat.

wrong.1: Transform[] is an array of managed objects; you cannot pass it to a job.
wrong.2: One thread for everything means no parallelism, and Transform is not available in an IJob anyway.
wrong.3: Schedule on an IJobFor runs everything on one worker thread; ScheduleParallel is the parallel one. And Transform is not available there either.

cards.q: Fill in the blanks: a parallel job whose run mode is picked at the call site.
cards.explain: IJob has no Execute(int). The index in Execute is always an int. A call with a length, a batchSize and a dependency is ScheduleParallel: Schedule on an IJobFor takes no batchSize and runs everything on one thread.

lessons.title: Schedule, Run, Complete
lessons.sub: When a job really runs, and why Complete() right after Schedule() is a mistake

cards.title: Schedule queues the job and returns a JobHandle
cards.body:
Schedule() does not run the job. It copies the job struct, puts it in a queue and immediately returns a JobHandle — a receipt you later use to wait for the result or to make another job depend on this one.

A detail not everyone knows: by default the job goes into a local queue and the worker threads do not see it yet. Unity batches jobs on purpose, because waking threads is expensive. The work reaches the workers when you call JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() or Complete().

So between Schedule() and Complete() the main thread is free — that gap is the whole point of jobs.

cards.title: Run, Schedule, Complete — three verbs
cards.body:
Run() executes Execute right away, on the same thread, with no queue and no parallelism. Under Burst it is still fast, and it is handy for debugging and for small data.

Schedule() — put it in the queue and get a JobHandle.

Complete() — wait. It raises the priority of the job and all its dependencies, and if no worker has picked the job up yet, it runs it right on the calling thread. Complete() also clears the safety system marks on the containers: until the job is completed with Complete(), the main thread may not read or write its data.

handle.IsCompleted only tells you whether the job has finished; it does not replace Complete().
cards.code:
job.Run();                        // here and now, on this thread
JobHandle h = job.Schedule(n, 64); // queued
// ... the main thread does its own work ...
h.Complete();                     // wait; the data is safe to read

cards.q: What do you get if you call Complete() on the very next line after Schedule()?
options: The speed of Run() plus the scheduling overhead: no parallelism with the main thread
Double speed: the main thread helps the workers
A safety system exception
The job runs next frame
cards.explain: Between Schedule() and Complete() the main thread does nothing, so it just waits. An IJobParallelFor still spreads its iterations over the workers, but the main thread idles the whole time, and you paid for queueing. There is no safety error here — it is not a race, it is lost parallelism.

wrong.1: Complete() can indeed run the job on the main thread, but that gains nothing: the main thread did none of its own work.
wrong.2: You get an exception when you touch the job data before Complete(). Here the order is right, just pointless.
wrong.3: Complete() blocks until the job is done, right now.

cards.title: Schedule early, complete late
cards.body:
The rule: schedule early, complete late. Schedule the job as soon as its input is ready, and call Complete() as late as you can — when you actually need the result.

The classic example from Unity’s docs: Schedule() in Update, Complete() in LateUpdate. In between run every other script’s Update, animation and physics — and all that time the worker threads compute your job.

Keep the JobHandle in a field for that. Right after Schedule() call JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs(), or the job may sit in the local queue until Complete().

cards.q: Which line kills parallelism in this frame?
cards.explain: Complete() comes right after Schedule(), so UpdateAI and UpdateUI wait for the job to end. Move Complete() to where the result is needed — LateUpdate, or at least after UpdateAI and UpdateUI — and the main thread works in parallel with the workers.

cards.q: What is true about Complete()? Pick all that apply.
options: If the job has not started, it may run right on the thread that called Complete()
Complete() also completes every job this one depends on
If you check handle.IsCompleted, you do not have to call Complete()
Until Complete() is called, the main thread must not read or write the job’s data
Complete() returns the job’s result
cards.explain: Complete() raises the priority of the job and its dependencies and may run it on the calling thread. Until it is called, the safety system treats the data as busy, and reading it on the main thread throws in the editor. IsCompleted only reports readiness: Complete() is still needed, it clears the safety system marks. Complete() returns no result — the result sits in the container you passed into the job.

cards.task: Rewrite Scaler so the job runs in parallel with the rest of the frame: Schedule in Update, Complete and Use(output) in LateUpdate. Keep the JobHandle in a field and wake the worker threads right after Schedule.

checks.label: The JobHandle is a field of the class, not a local of Update
JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() is called right after Schedule
There is a LateUpdate method that calls Complete()
Use(output) is called in LateUpdate after Complete()
Update has no Complete()

cards.explain: The job starts in Update while the rest of the frame’s scripts run, and by LateUpdate it is usually done — Complete() just collects the result.

cards.title: So why Run()
cards.body:
Run() is not a “bad Schedule”. It is the same job and the same Burst code, executed here and now on the current thread.

It fits when the data is small and queueing costs more than the work, when you need the result immediately, and when debugging: the order of execution becomes predictable while the Burst code stays Burst code.

If you are going to write Schedule() and then Complete() right away anyway, write Run() instead: same meaning, no scheduling.
cards.code:
// small data, result needed right now
new ScaleJob { input = input, output = output, k = 2f }.Run(input.Length);

cards.q: Put one “schedule early, complete late” frame in order.
items: Update: gather the input into a NativeArray
Update: job.Schedule() and JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs()
Other Updates, animation, physics — the workers compute the job
LateUpdate: handle.Complete()
LateUpdate: read the result and apply it
cards.explain: The data is ready — schedule the job at once and wake the threads. Everything between Update and LateUpdate runs in parallel. Complete() comes last, right before reading the result.

cards.task: Fix Update: the result is read before the job has finished, and the array is freed while the job may still write to it. Add the missing call in the right place.

checks.label: Complete() is called on the JobHandle
Complete() comes before reading result[0]
Complete() comes before result.Dispose()
The array is still freed with Dispose()

cards.explain: In the editor the safety system would catch reading result[0] before Complete() with an exception. A build has no such checks: you would read garbage, and Dispose() would free memory the job is still writing. Here you have to wait at once because the result is needed in this same Update; when you can, move the read to LateUpdate.

cards.q: Interviewer: “Your job takes 2 ms, you Schedule in Update and Complete in LateUpdate, yet the profiler shows LateUpdate waiting 2 ms.” What do you check first?
options: Whether JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() is called after Schedule: without it the job may have sat in the local queue until Complete()
Whether Burst is on — Complete() does not work without it
Whether batchSize is 1
Whether there are too many worker threads
cards.explain: If the worker threads were never woken, the job starts only in Complete(), and all 2 ms land on LateUpdate. Check ScheduleBatchedJobs first, then look at the profiler Timeline to see when the job actually started on the workers.

lessons.title: Final: Jobs and Burst basics
lessons.sub: Threads and the compiler, HPC#, kinds of jobs and a frame with Schedule and Complete — no hints

cards.q: Say it out loud: “How is the Job System different from Burst?” Which answer would you give?
options: They are two independent things. The Job System spreads work over worker threads, respects dependencies and catches races in the Editor. Burst is a compiler: HPC# through LLVM into native code with SIMD. Together you get parallel code that is fast on every thread, and Burst also works without jobs, on a static method
Burst is a newer version of the Job System with multithreading support
The Job System exists so that Burst can work: without jobs Burst is not used
They are the same thing: Burst is an attribute that turns on worker threads
cards.explain: A strong answer separates the axes: threads versus machine code. Plus two signs of experience — the four combinations (Burst without jobs exists) and “profile first”.

wrong.1: Burst is a compiler, not a scheduler. It creates no threads.
wrong.2: Burst also compiles static methods called from the main thread, and Run() with no worker threads.
wrong.3: Worker threads come from Schedule(); [BurstCompile] only changes what code Execute runs as.

cards.q: Which of these will Burst not compile? Pick all that apply.
options: A string title field in a job struct
A local List<int> variable inside Execute
float3 p = math.normalize(v) inside Execute
A FixedString64Bytes title field
A Func<int, int> field in a job struct
A [ReadOnly] NativeArray<int> field
cards.explain: A string, a List and a delegate are managed objects, and HPC# has none. Unity.Mathematics, FixedString and native containers are exactly the Burst-friendly replacements.

cards.q: Match the task with the job type.
pairs: The same code, sometimes on the main thread for debugging, sometimes in parallel
Visit every entity with LocalTransform and Speed components

cards.q: Which line throws a safety-system exception in the Editor?
cards.explain: The job that writes positions is still running while the main thread already reads positions[0]. In the Editor the safety system stops this with an exception; in a build you would read a half-written element. Read it in LateUpdate after Complete().

cards.q: Trap: an IJobFor is started with job.Schedule(n, default). The profiler shows all the work on one worker thread. Why?
options: Schedule on an IJobFor runs all iterations in order on one worker thread; ScheduleParallel is the parallel one
[BurstCompile] is missing
The batchSize is too small
IJobFor cannot run in parallel at all
cards.explain: IJobFor has three modes: Run — the main thread, Schedule — one worker thread, ScheduleParallel — batches on several. The job type is the same; the call picks the mode.

wrong.1: Burst changes the code, not the number of threads.
wrong.2: Schedule on an IJobFor has no batchSize at all.
wrong.3: It can — through ScheduleParallel.

cards.q: An input check in a Burst job must give a clear error in the Editor and must not crash the player build. How do you do it?
options: Put the throw in a method marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")] and call it from Execute
Wrap Execute in try/catch
Leave the throw in Execute: in a build safety checks switch it off
Call Debug.LogError instead of throw and carry on
cards.explain: In the Editor the symbol is defined, so the check runs and throws. In a player build the method and its calls disappear. An ordinary throw from Burst code in a player build is an abort.

wrong.1: Burst does not support catch.
wrong.2: Safety checks are unavailable in player builds, and an ordinary throw stays there and aborts the app.
wrong.3: You can log, but then the code goes on with bad data — that is a warning, not a check.

cards.q: A static method with [BurstCompile] is called from the main thread. What did you get?
options: Native Burst code on the same main thread — no parallelism, but faster than managed code
Work on the worker threads, like a job
Nothing: Burst only works inside jobs
An automatic call through Schedule()
cards.explain: That is combination 3: Burst without worker threads. The declaring type must be marked [BurstCompile] too, the method is not generic, structs go by ref, in or pointer, and it pays to hand such a call a whole batch of work.

wrong.1: Only the Job System gives you threads; a direct call runs where it was made.
wrong.2: Burst compiles static methods too.
wrong.3: A direct call is an ordinary method call, with no queue.

cards.task: Write HealJob : IJobFor with [BurstCompile]: fields hp (NativeArray<float>), regen ([ReadOnly] NativeArray<float>), float dt and float maxHp. Execute(int i) adds regen[i] * dt to hp[i] and caps the result with math.min(…, maxHp). In Healing.Schedule create the job and return the handle from ScheduleParallel(hp.Length, 64, dependsOn).

checks.label: HealJob is an IJobFor struct with [BurstCompile]
regen is a [ReadOnly] NativeArray<float>
Execute(int i) writes hp[i] using math.min
There is no for loop in Execute
ScheduleParallel(hp.Length, batchSize, dependsOn) is called
The method does not return dependsOn instead of the job’s handle

cards.explain: One iteration is one element, with no loop and no foreign indices, so the job splits into batches safely. ScheduleParallel hands batches of 64 to the worker threads, and the caller passes the returned handle on as a dependency or waits on it with Complete(). Return dependsOn and nobody ever waits for HealJob itself.

cards.task: Finish Mover: VelocityJob : IJobParallelForTransform with [BurstCompile] moves transform.position by velocity[index] * dt (velocity is a [ReadOnly] NativeArray<Vector3>, dt is a float). In Update schedule the job over the transforms field and wake the workers right away; call Complete() in LateUpdate.

checks.label: VelocityJob is an IJobParallelForTransform struct with [BurstCompile]
Execute(int index, TransformAccess transform)
velocity is a [ReadOnly] NativeArray<Vector3>
In Update: Schedule(transforms), then JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs()
LateUpdate calls Complete()
There is no Complete() in Update

cards.explain: The transforms move on worker threads while the rest of the frame’s Update calls run, and LateUpdate collects the finished work. ScheduleBatchedJobs keeps the job from sitting in the local queue until Complete(). And remember the hierarchy: under a shared root the read-write Schedule runs everything on one thread.

cards.q: Build the answer to “How would you speed up a hot loop?”
items: Find the hot spot in the profiler
Move the data into native containers and structs
Move the loop body into an IJobFor and mark it [BurstCompile]
ScheduleParallel in Update, Complete() in LateUpdate
Measure again: the profiler Timeline and the Burst Inspector
cards.explain: Measure — data — a Burst job — schedule early, complete late — measure again. That sequence is the answer that tells the interviewer you have done it yourself.

cards.title: Practice in Unity
cards.body:
A 30–60 minute task. Unity 6 with the Burst, Collections and Mathematics packages. One component moves 200,000 points every frame: NativeArray<float3> positions and velocities, allocated in Awake with Allocator.Persistent and freed in OnDestroy.

Steps.
1. A loop in Update on the main thread — note the Update time in the Profiler.
2. The same loop in an IJob without Burst: Schedule() and right away Complete().
3. Add [BurstCompile]. In the Editor turn on Jobs > Burst > Synchronous Compilation, or the first frames run without Burst.
4. Switch to IJobFor and ScheduleParallel(Count, 64, default).
5. Spread it across the frame: Schedule and JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() in Update, Complete() in LateUpdate.

What to measure. In the Profiler (CPU Usage, Timeline view): main-thread and worker-thread time for every step, and in LateUpdate how long Complete() waits (the WaitForJobGroupID marker). In the Burst Inspector (Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector) find your job, turn on “Highlight SIMD Scalar vs Packed” and check which instructions the hot loop uses: packed (vmulps, vaddps) or scalar (vmulss, vaddss). Why an array of float3 vectorizes worse than separate float arrays is covered in unit 3.

How you know it worked. Step 3 is clearly faster than step 2 on the same single thread — that is Burst’s share; in step 4 the work shows up as bars on several worker threads; in step 5 the main thread barely waits in LateUpdate; the console shows no leak warnings. Take the final numbers in a Development build with the profiler attached, because the Editor runs safety checks. Write down a “step → ms” table — that is a ready-made story for the interview.

units.title: Data, safety and dependencies
units.blurb: How data gets into a job and back, the safety system and races, the dependency graph, allocators and leaks, writing from a parallel job and batchSize. This is where mid-levels drop out.

lessons.title: Data into a job and back
lessons.sub: A job works on a copy: what you can put in it and how to get the result out

cards.title: A job gets a copy of its struct
cards.body:
A job struct is a parcel of data for another thread. On Schedule() the job system copies it byte by byte, and Execute runs on that copy. Whatever the job writes to its plain fields stays in the copy, so after Complete() your original job variable is unchanged.

The same goes for Run(): the extension method takes the struct by value, so it works on a copy too.

This is the first data question in an interview: “why is the job’s field still zero after Complete()?” Because the job never wrote to your struct.

cards.q: You replaced job.Schedule().Complete() with job.Run(). What does Debug.Log(job.sum) print now?
options: 0: Run() gets a copy of the struct too
The sum: Run() executes the job on the same thread
A safety system exception
Garbage: the field is not initialized
cards.explain: Run() is an extension method, and the struct is passed to it by value. Same thread, but still its own copy, and the sum stays there. The thread does not matter; what matters is where the job writes.

wrong.1: Same thread, but the data is a copy: the extension method takes the struct by value.
wrong.2: This is neither a race nor access to a busy container. There is no error, only a lost result.
wrong.3: C# struct fields are always initialized: sum = 0, and it stays that way.

cards.title: Only blittable data in a job
cards.body:
Since the struct is copied byte by byte, it cannot hold references into the managed heap: a copied reference would point to an object the garbage collector may move and another thread may change. The docs say a job can only access blittable types. In practice the rule is unmanaged fields, no reference types. bool is not strictly blittable, but it works in jobs.

Allowed: numbers, Unity.Mathematics vectors, your own structs made of them, FixedString64Bytes and the other FixedString types, Native containers. Not allowed: T[], string, List<T>, classes, Transform and any UnityEngine object — Schedule() throws, and Burst will not compile such code.

A separate trap is mutable static fields. Nothing stops a non-Burst job from using them, but nothing protects them either: the docs warn plainly that it may crash your application. Burst rejects writes to statics, except through SharedStatic<T>.

cards.q: Which fields can go into a job struct? Pick all that apply.
options: NativeArray<float3> positions
float dt and int count
string name
int[] ids
FixedString64Bytes label
GameObject target
cards.explain: Native containers, numbers and FixedString are unmanaged and can be copied byte by byte. string, int[] and GameObject are references into the managed heap: Schedule() throws, and Burst will not compile it.

cards.title: Results only through a container
cards.body:
A Native container in a struct is a small struct holding a pointer to native memory. Copying the job copies the pointer, not the data, so the copy and the original look at the same memory. The docs say it directly: after the job finishes, only data written to a NativeContainer is accessible.

For a single value people used to take a NativeArray of length 1 — the manual’s example still does. Collections has NativeReference<T> for that: one value, a .Value property, clearer to read.

The order is always the same: allocate → pass to the job → Complete() → read → Dispose(). Allocator.TempJob is for data that lives up to a few frames; allocators get their own lesson in this unit.

A habit: accumulate in a local variable and write .Value once at the end. It reads better, and you do not depend on the compiler figuring out it can keep the sum in a register.
cards.deep: Inside a NativeArray<T> are a pointer, a length, an allocator and, in the Editor, a few safety system fields. Copying the job copies those few fields, so scheduling is cheap however many elements the array has.

cards.title: [ReadOnly] and [WriteOnly]
cards.body:
By default a container field in a job counts as read and write. To the safety system that job is a writer, and no other job may touch the container until the first one is done.

[ReadOnly] is a promise to only read. Per the docs it allows two jobs to run in parallel and read the same container. Writing to a [ReadOnly] container throws in the Editor.

[WriteOnly] means write only; reading such a container also throws in the Editor.

The rule: mark everything a job only reads as [ReadOnly]. It is the cheapest way to let the scheduler run jobs in parallel. And remember it is a promise checked only in the Editor; in a build it does not make the data immutable.

cards.q: Build a job that counts positive ids and returns the number through a container
cards.explain: The job only reads ids — [ReadOnly]. One number comes back through a NativeReference<int>, written to count.Value. NativeArray has no Value property, and [WriteOnly] on ids would break the reads.

cards.q: Which line throws in the Editor?
cards.explain: hp is marked [ReadOnly], but the job writes to it. In the Editor a write to a [ReadOnly] container is caught with an exception. Remove the attribute from hp: the job both reads and writes it.

cards.q: Two jobs read positions, but neither marks it [ReadOnly]. They are scheduled with no dependency on each other. What happens in the Editor?
options: An exception on the second Schedule: without [ReadOnly] both count as writers
Nothing: they only read
The second job automatically waits for the first
An exception in Execute when the second job reads positions
cards.explain: The safety system does not look at what a job actually does — it looks at the declarations. A field without [ReadOnly] is write access, and two independent writers of one container are caught as soon as the second is scheduled. Mark positions [ReadOnly] in both jobs and they run in parallel.

wrong.1: The safety system judges by declarations, not by the code in Execute. Without [ReadOnly] the field is write access.
wrong.2: The job system never adds dependencies on its own: you pass them explicitly, or you get an exception.
wrong.3: The conflict is caught earlier, when the second job is scheduled, before it starts running.

cards.task: Fix Stats.Sum: the sum is always 0. In SumJob replace the float sum field with NativeReference<float> result, mark input [ReadOnly] and write the sum to result.Value. In Sum create result with Allocator.TempJob, after Complete() store result.Value in a local variable, dispose of result and return the sum.

checks.label: The input NativeArray<float> is marked [ReadOnly]
SumJob has a NativeReference<float> field
Execute writes the sum to .Value
SumJob has no plain float field for the result
The NativeReference is created with Allocator.TempJob
After Complete(), .Value is read into a variable, then Dispose() is called

cards.explain: The job writes to native memory that both the copy and the original NativeReference point to, so after Complete() the value is visible to the main thread. Read first, then Dispose(): after disposal you may not read .Value. In an interview: “a job gets a copy of its struct; results come back only through a container — for a single value, a NativeReference.”

cards.q: Interviewer: “Why can’t you return a result through a plain job field, while a NativeArray works?”
options: Schedule copies the struct; a copy of a container is the same pointer to native memory, so writes through it are visible after Complete()
NativeArray is a class, so it is passed by reference
Fields are copied back only for jobs without Burst
A field works too if you call Run() instead of Schedule()
cards.explain: The short answer: the job is a copy, a container is a pointer. Both get copied, but a copied pointer leads to the same memory. That is why a job’s output is always a container: NativeArray, NativeReference and the rest.

wrong.1: NativeArray is a struct. The copies share memory because there is a pointer inside.
wrong.2: Burst has nothing to do with it: fields are never copied back.
wrong.3: Run() takes the struct by value as well.

lessons.title: The safety system and races
lessons.sub: What the Editor catches, why a build stays silent, and what the opt-out attributes cost

cards.title: The safety system: who touches what
cards.body:
In the Editor every Native container carries a hidden safety handle, an AtomicSafetyHandle. The field exists only under the ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS define, which the Editor has.

On Schedule() the job system records which job reads and which job writes which containers — from the struct’s fields and the [ReadOnly] / [WriteOnly] attributes. Every later schedule and every main-thread access to a container is checked against those marks. Complete() clears them.

The key point: the check does not catch a race as it happens, it checks whether a race is possible from the declarations. So the error shows up on the very first run, even if on your machine the threads would never have collided.

cards.title: What gets caught, and with what
cards.body:
The four situations interviewers ask about most:

  1. Two independent jobs touch one container and at least one of them writes: InvalidOperationException on the second Schedule(). The message even names the cure — make the first job a dependency of the second. Two readers with [ReadOnly] do not get in each other’s way.
  2. The main thread touches data of a pending job. You may not read while a job that writes the container is unfinished. You may not write while any job that reads or writes it is unfinished. Also an InvalidOperationException.
  3. A write to a [ReadOnly] container inside a job — InvalidOperationException.
  4. An IJobParallelFor writes outside its own range of iterations — IndexOutOfRangeException. The rule is simple: in a parallel job, write only to element [i].

cards.q: Which line throws in the Editor?
cards.explain: MoveJob writes pos and is not finished yet — Complete() comes only in LateUpdate. The main thread writes to the same container, and the safety system throws an InvalidOperationException. Move the write before Schedule or after Complete().

cards.q: MoveJob writes pos. CenterJob only reads pos and marks it [ReadOnly]. Both are scheduled with no dependency. What happens in the Editor?
options: An InvalidOperationException when CenterJob is scheduled: a reader was scheduled while a writer is unfinished
Nothing: [ReadOnly] allows parallel reads
CenterJob automatically waits for MoveJob
An exception only in a build
cards.explain: [ReadOnly] lets readers run in parallel with each other. A reader next to an unfinished writer is a race: CenterJob may read half-updated positions. The cure is a dependency: schedule CenterJob with MoveJob’s handle.

wrong.1: In parallel only with other readers. If someone writes, the reader needs a dependency on it.
wrong.2: The job system does not add dependencies by itself — it throws and tells you which one to add.
wrong.3: A build has no checks at all: there you get a silent race, not an exception.

cards.title: Why a build stays silent
cards.body:
Safety system checks are unavailable in a build, not “off by default”: their code exists only under ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS, and it does not make it into a standalone player — a Development Build (the one with the profiler and debugging) included. No safety handle, nothing to check against.

The same racy code in a build simply runs: one job reads the positions while another has rewritten half of them. The result is silent data corruption: jittering units, the odd NaN, bugs that show up once in a hundred runs and depend on the device’s core count.

Exceptions in Burst code come with the same warning: in the Editor a throw is caught and logged to the console, but in a build it aborts the application. Mark your own checks [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")] so they leave the build together with Unity’s.

The takeaway: every safety system exception in the Editor is a bug that becomes data corruption in a build. You fix it, you do not silence it.
cards.deep: A small subset of checks can be enabled in a player with the UNITY_DOTS_DEBUG define. It is a part of the checks, not the same set as in the Editor, so races are still hunted in the Editor.

cards.q: What is true about races and checks in a build? Pick all that apply.
options: A build has no safety system checks: their code is not compiled into the player
A race in a build means silent data corruption and rare, hard-to-reproduce bugs
A Development Build runs the same checks as the Editor
A throw in Burst code without [Conditional] aborts the application in a build
If the Editor never threw a single exception, the code has no races
cards.explain: The checks exist only under ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS and do not reach the player — a Development Build is no exception. A throw in Burst code is an abort in a build. And the absence of exceptions only speaks for the code paths that actually ran in the Editor with checks on.

cards.title: Where it is switched on
cards.body:
Two different switches, often confused:

  • Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Enable Jobs Debugger — the job system checks: conflicts between jobs and with the main thread. From code, JobsUtility.JobDebuggerEnabled, which only has an effect in the Editor.
  • Jobs > Burst > Enable Safety Checks — Off / On / Force On — the checks inside Burst code (out-of-bounds access, writes to [ReadOnly], the parallel job’s range). It always goes back to On after an Editor reload.

For a single job there is [BurstCompile(DisableSafetyChecks = true)]; Force On overrides that too.

Checks are extra code on every container access. That is why performance is measured in a build, not in the Editor with checks on. And turning checks off to “make the exception go away” means hiding a race.

cards.title: Opt-out attributes and what they cost
cards.body:
Sometimes the safety system is too strict for correct code. That is what these attributes are for:

  • [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction] — a parallel job may write to other indices. Used for scatter writes when there is no overlap by construction.
  • [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction] — no checks at all for this field.
  • [NativeDisableUnsafePtrRestriction] — allows a pointer field in a job.

The cost: an attribute does not make code safe, it removes the net and puts the proof on you. A race stops being an exception in the Editor and becomes silent everywhere. And Burst treats fields with [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction] as possibly aliasing, which may cost optimizations.

The order: first a dependency, [ReadOnly] or splitting the data; an attribute only with a comment explaining why there is no race.

cards.q: Match each situation with what happens or what you need
pairs: An IJobParallelFor writes to an element outside its range
Two independent jobs write to one array
The same race in a build
You must write to other indices, with no overlap by construction

cards.title: Fix it with a dependency, not an opt-out
cards.body:
The exception message tells you what to do: pass the previously scheduled job as a dependency of the new one. The last parameter of Schedule is JobHandle dependsOn: the new job will not start until the dependency has finished. The safety system sees the order and stays quiet.

The main thread does not wait here — unlike Complete() between jobs. The worker threads wait, and only for each other.

Other honest fixes: merge the two steps into one job, or give each job its own container (a double buffer). How to build a whole frame’s graph out of dependencies is the next lesson.

cards.task: In Swarm, CenterJob reads pos while MoveJob writes it, and in the Editor Schedule throws. Fix it with a dependency: pass MoveJob’s handle to avg.Schedule and mark pos in CenterJob [ReadOnly]. Keep Complete() in LateUpdate and do not use opt-out attributes.

checks.label: CenterJob is scheduled with a dependency on MoveJob’s handle
In CenterJob the pos field is marked [ReadOnly]
No NativeDisable…Restriction attributes
No Complete() in Update
In LateUpdate Complete() comes before reading center.Value

cards.explain: With the dependency CenterJob starts only after MoveJob, and completing the single last handle in LateUpdate completes both. [ReadOnly] is not required by the safety system here, but it describes the access honestly and lets other readers of pos run in parallel with CenterJob. In an interview: “a safety system exception is a race; I fix it with a dependency, not by turning the checks off.”

cards.q: Interviewer: “In the Editor everything is clean, but in an Android build units sometimes jitter. The positions job has [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction].” What do you suspect first?
options: A race: the attribute hid it in the Editor, and a build has no checks at all — one job reads the positions while another writes them
Different float precision on ARM
A batchSize that is too small
A Burst bug on Android
cards.explain: A classic: the check was disabled because “the exception was in the way”. The Editor went quiet, the build never had checks, and the phone’s core count and timings differ — so the race surfaced. Remove the attribute, look at the exception in the Editor and fix it with a dependency.

wrong.1: Float differences do happen, but an opt-out attribute on the positions container is a far likelier cause.
wrong.2: batchSize affects speed, not data correctness.
wrong.3: Blaming the compiler is the last resort when the code has race checks turned off.

lessons.title: Dependencies and the job graph
lessons.sub: dependsOn, CombineDependencies and a frame pipeline without needless waits

cards.title: dependsOn: a job waits for a job, not for the main thread
cards.body:
The last parameter of every Schedule is JobHandle dependsOn. A job with a dependency sits in the queue until the dependency has finished and starts right after it — on a worker thread, with no help from the main thread.

The returned handle stands for this job together with all its dependencies. In the docs’ words, completing a dependent job must first complete any job it depends on, and any jobs those depend on. So at the end of a chain one Complete() on the last handle is enough.

default(JobHandle) means “no dependency”; that is what the default parameter is.
cards.deep: A graph can cross a frame boundary: if the result is only needed next frame, keep the handle in a field and pass it to the first job of the next frame as dependsOn. You still need Complete() before the main thread touches the data — it is also what clears the safety system marks. And remember the manual’s advice: a job should fit within a frame.

cards.title: A graph: CombineDependencies
cards.body:
A chain is a special case. In a real frame a job often waits for several others: that is fan-in. For it, JobHandle.CombineDependencies merges handles into one that completes when all of them have. Overloads: two handles, three, a NativeArray<JobHandle> and a NativeSlice<JobHandle>. Do not confuse it with JobHandle.CompleteAll — that one does not merge, it waits on the main thread.

The reverse is fan-out: one handle is passed to several jobs. They run in parallel if they do not conflict: the shared container is only read ([ReadOnly]), and each writes its own.

The building rule: a dependency is about data. A job depends on every unfinished job that writes what it reads, and on every job that touches what it writes.

cards.q: What is true about job dependencies? Pick all that apply.
options: Complete() on the last handle completes the whole chain before it
CombineDependencies takes two or three handles, or a NativeArray<JobHandle>
A job scheduled with dependsOn blocks the main thread until the dependency finishes
Two jobs with the same dependency that only read a shared array ([ReadOnly]) and each write their own can run in parallel
The job system adds a dependency by itself between jobs that touch the same container
cards.explain: The worker threads wait; the main thread is free until Complete(). The last job’s handle pulls the whole chain along. The job system never invents dependencies: if some are missing, the safety system throws.

cards.title: A frame pipeline: positions → spatial hash → collisions → transforms
cards.body:
A typical crowd or flock frame is a chain where each link reads the previous link’s output:

  1. MoveJob integrates positions from velocities.
  2. HashJob is the spatial hash: for each agent it computes a grid cell, so neighbours are searched only nearby. In a real project this also fills a hash map or sorts by cell — parallel writing has its own lesson.
  3. CollideJob looks at neighbours by cell and writes new velocities.
  4. ApplyJob is an IJobParallelForTransform over a TransformAccessArray: it copies positions into Transforms straight from the worker threads.

The idiom: one variable h that becomes the new link’s handle at every step. Only the last one goes into a class field, and there is one Complete(), in LateUpdate.

cards.q: Put the links of the frame in order.
items: MoveJob: new positions from velocities
HashJob: a grid cell for each agent
CollideJob: neighbours by cell → new velocities
ApplyJob: positions into Transforms via TransformAccessArray
LateUpdate: one Complete() on the last handle
cards.explain: Each link reads what the previous one wrote, so each depends on the previous one. The main thread schedules the whole chain at once and waits once — at the end.

cards.title: Anti-pattern: Complete() between links
cards.body:
If you complete each link before scheduling the next, the main thread turns into a babysitter:

  • every Complete() blocks the main thread — in the Profiler these are WaitForJobGroupID blocks;
  • while the main thread wakes up and schedules the next job, the workers idle — gaps appear between the links;
  • the whole chain’s time comes out of the main thread’s frame instead of running alongside it.

With dependencies the whole chain is queued at once: a worker picks up the next link as soon as the previous one ends, and the main thread is free until the single Complete().

The only honest reason to wait midway is that the main thread needs a number to decide what to schedule next. Even then, think first: the decision can move into a job, and for a length known only after the previous step there is IJobParallelForDefer over a NativeList’s length.

cards.q: Which line breaks the pipeline?
cards.explain: h.Complete() in the middle of Update makes the main thread wait for MoveJob and HashJob, although CollideJob is scheduled with a dependency on h anyway. Delete the line — the dependency already guarantees the order, and there will be one Complete(), in LateUpdate.

cards.q: CollideJob is scheduled with a dependency on HashJob, while desired is written by SteerJob, scheduled separately. What happens in the Editor?
options: An InvalidOperationException when CollideJob is scheduled: it reads desired, and SteerJob, which writes it, is not among its dependencies
Nothing: CollideJob waits for all jobs scheduled earlier anyway
CollideJob waits for SteerJob because both touch desired
An exception when SteerJob is scheduled
cards.explain: The dependency on HashJob pulls MoveJob along, but not SteerJob — it is a separate branch. The safety system sees an unfinished writer of desired and throws. The fix is a fan-in: JobHandle.CombineDependencies(hash, steer) as CollideJob’s dependsOn.

wrong.1: A job waits only for what is passed in dependsOn and their dependencies. Nobody waits for “everything earlier”.
wrong.2: Dependencies are not inferred from data — you declare them, and the safety system checks whether they are enough.
wrong.3: SteerJob is the first of the jobs touching desired to be scheduled; it has nothing to conflict with.

cards.q: Fix the graph: CollideJob must wait for both HashJob and SteerJob
cards.explain: CombineDependencies merges the two branches into one handle, and it goes into CollideJob’s dependsOn. CompleteAll would wait on the main thread, and passing only steer or only hash would lose a branch again.

cards.task: In Crowd three jobs are completed one by one right in Update. Turn them into a chain: hash.Schedule depends on the move handle, collide.Schedule on the hash handle; store the last handle in the handle field and wake the worker threads. Complete() goes only in LateUpdate.

checks.label: hash.Schedule gets the handle from move.Schedule as a dependency
collide.Schedule gets the handle from hash.Schedule as a dependency
The handle from collide.Schedule is stored in the handle field
JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() is called after the chain is scheduled
No Complete() in Update
LateUpdate calls handle.Complete()

cards.explain: The main thread schedules the three jobs as one batch and moves on. The workers run them back to back with no gaps, and Complete() on the last handle in LateUpdate completes the whole chain. In an interview: “I build dependencies from the data: whoever reads another job’s output depends on its writer; one Complete(), at the end.”

cards.q: Interviewer: “Why a dependency graph? You could just complete the jobs one by one — it’s easier to follow.”
options: Every Complete() blocks the main thread and leaves the workers idle between links; with dependencies the chain runs back to back on the workers, and the main thread is free until one Complete() at the end
Complete() may not be called more than once per frame
Without dependencies Burst does not compile the job
Dependencies are only needed for IJobParallelFor
cards.explain: The answer has two parts: main-thread time (wait once, not at every link) and worker utilization (no gaps while the main thread schedules the next job). On top of that, dependencies are what the safety system demands from jobs that share data.

wrong.1: You may call it as often as you like — it just costs main-thread time.
wrong.2: Burst compiles the job’s code and knows nothing about the graph.
wrong.3: Every kind of job has dependsOn in its Schedule.

lessons.title: Allocators and leaks
lessons.sub: Temp, TempJob and Persistent, how to find a forgotten Dispose, and why a long-lived buffer is allocated once

cards.title: The garbage collector does not see native memory
cards.body:
NativeArray, NativeList, NativeReference and the other native containers live outside the managed heap. The struct itself is a pointer, a length and (in the Editor) a safety system handle; a copy of the struct points to the same memory. That is exactly why you can hand them to a job.

The flip side: the garbage collector never frees that memory. Every allocation has to be closed with Dispose(), otherwise it is a leak that will not go away on its own.

When you create a container you pick an allocator. It decides how fast the allocation is, how long the memory lives and which checks Unity runs for you.

cards.title: Temp, TempJob, Persistent
cards.body:
Allocator.Temp is the fastest. Every frame the main thread creates a Temp allocator and releases it in full at the end of the frame; each job gets its own Temp per thread, released at the end of the job. You do not need to call Dispose() — it does nothing.

Allocator.TempJob is slower than Temp and faster than Persistent. It is for data that goes into a job. Free it within 4 frames, or the Editor complains: the Unity Manual calls it a warning, the Collections docs say native containers throw an exception.

Allocator.Persistent is a wrapper over malloc: the slowest allocation and no lifetime checks at all, the memory lives until you call Dispose(). “Slow” is about allocating, not about access: reading and writing that memory is just as fast.
flow: Temp → until the end of the frame or job
TempJob → into a job, Dispose within ≤ 4 frames
cards.code:
var perFrame = new NativeArray<int>(64, Allocator.Temp);      // main thread, this frame only
var forJob   = new NativeArray<int>(n, Allocator.TempJob);    // into a job, Dispose within 4 frames
var longLive = new NativeArray<int>(n, Allocator.Persistent); // until you call Dispose

cards.q: A one-off buffer: filled in Update, processed by a job and read in LateUpdate of the same frame. Which allocator?
options: Allocator.TempJob
Allocator.Temp — it lives until the end of the frame anyway
Allocator.Persistent — it is the most reliable
Any: the allocator only affects speed
cards.explain: The data goes into a job and lives for less than 4 frames — that is exactly TempJob. Main-thread Temp cannot be passed into a job. Persistent here is the slowest allocation with no lifetime check: forget the Dispose and you get a silent leak.

wrong.1: Main-thread Temp memory cannot be passed into a job: in the Editor Schedule() throws an exception.
wrong.2: It works, but it is the slowest allocation, and nothing reminds you of a forgotten Dispose() after 4 frames.
wrong.3: The allocator sets the lifetime, the checks, and whether the memory may go into a job at all.

cards.title: Temp inside a job — yes; main-thread Temp into a job — no
cards.body:
Allocating Allocator.Temp inside Execute is fine and encouraged: every job on every thread has its own Temp allocator, and everything allocated is released at the end of the job. It is the best choice for a temporary neighbour list, a traversal stack or an intermediate array — fast and leak-free.

The reverse is forbidden: main-thread Temp memory cannot be passed into a job. It is released at the end of the frame and the job may outlive the frame, so in the Editor Schedule() throws an exception. For data that goes into a job use TempJob or Persistent.

cards.q: Which line is the bug?
cards.explain: cells is allocated from main-thread Temp and passed into a job. In the Editor Schedule() throws an exception. Use TempJob (and Dispose after Complete) or a Persistent buffer allocated once.

cards.q: Match each allocator with its property
pairs: No Dispose needed: released at the end of the frame or job
For a job; free it within 4 frames
A wrapper over malloc, lives until Dispose
Cannot be passed into a job

cards.title: A long-lived buffer: allocate it once
cards.body:
A buffer you need every frame should not be allocated every frame. Even TempJob means an allocation and a free every frame, plus one more place to forget a Dispose().

The pattern: allocate Persistent once in Awake (or OnEnable), reuse it every frame, free it in OnDestroy (or OnDisable). On a NativeList, Clear() resets the length but keeps the capacity — no reallocation.

Before Dispose(), finish the pending job with Complete(): OnDestroy can arrive while this frame’s job has not been collected yet, and then the job would write into freed memory. IsCreated guards against a second Dispose() and against a buffer that was never allocated.

cards.task: Boids allocates a TempJob buffer in every Update and frees it in LateUpdate. Rework it: allocate velocities once in Awake with Allocator.Persistent, reuse it every frame and free it in OnDestroy — after Complete() on the pending job.

checks.label: Awake allocates the buffer with Allocator.Persistent
There is no new NativeArray in Update
There is no Dispose() in Update or LateUpdate
There is an OnDestroy, and it calls Dispose()
In OnDestroy, Complete() comes before Dispose()

cards.explain: One allocation for the component’s whole life instead of an allocation and a free every frame, and a single place where the memory is freed. Complete() in OnDestroy is needed because this frame’s job may still be running: in the Editor the safety system catches a Dispose() under a live job, in a build the job would write into freed memory. In the interview: “long-lived buffers are Persistent, I allocate them in Awake and free them in OnDestroy after Complete”.

cards.title: Free it after the job: Dispose(JobHandle)
cards.body:
If a temporary buffer is only needed by jobs, there is no reason to wait on the main thread just to call Dispose(). Dispose(JobHandle) schedules the free as one more job that runs after the given one, and returns its JobHandle.

That way a TempJob buffer lives exactly as long as the chain that needs it, and the main thread never blocks. The old way is the [DeallocateOnJobCompletion] attribute on a job field: it still works, but only for NativeArray. For Collections containers use Dispose(JobHandle).

cards.title: Leak detection: where did it leak
cards.body:
Unity tracks native allocations and reports the forgotten ones. The level is in Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Leak Detection Level, or in code via NativeLeakDetection.Mode:

  • Disabled — no tracking;
  • Enabled — report leaks; this is the default in the Editor and in development builds, while a regular build defaults to Disabled;
  • EnabledWithStackTrace — also the call stack where the memory was allocated; it works only in the Editor and development builds, and capturing a stack for every allocation is expensive — turn it on while you hunt.

Forgotten memory is reported when the script domain unloads, not at the moment of the leak. So a report without a stack tells you little: switch to EnabledWithStackTrace, reproduce, and see where it was allocated. The “TempJob older than 4 frames” check works separately from this.
cards.code:
// Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Leak Detection Level, or from code:
NativeLeakDetection.Mode = NativeLeakDetectionMode.EnabledWithStackTrace;
cards.deep: There are more allocators than the classic three. Allocator.Domain (in the engine since Unity 2023.1) lives as long as the script domain. Collections 2.x adds AllocatorManager and custom allocators such as RewindableAllocator: many allocations, then one fast rewind instead of many frees. In Entities a world has a WorldUpdateAllocator — a double buffer whose allocations live for two frames, need no manual free and can be passed into jobs.

cards.q: What is true about native memory leaks? Select all.
options: The garbage collector will eventually free a forgotten NativeArray
EnabledWithStackTrace shows where the leaked memory was allocated
Dispose() on a Temp allocation does nothing
Persistent gets the same lifetime check as TempJob
In a regular (non-development) build, leak detection is off by default
cards.explain: Native memory is outside the managed heap; the GC never frees it. Only EnabledWithStackTrace gives you the allocation stack. Temp is released in full at the end of the frame or job, so Dispose() on it is a no-op. Persistent has no lifetime checks: a forgotten buffer only shows up as a leak at domain unload. A regular build defaults to Disabled.

cards.q: Interviewer: “Why not just allocate everything as Persistent and stop thinking about it?”
options: Persistent is the slowest allocation with no lifetime checks. For short-lived buffers TempJob is faster and flags a forgotten Dispose after 4 frames, and for scratch data inside a job there is Temp. Persistent is for buffers you allocate once and reuse
Persistent memory is slower to read and write in a job: it sits further from the cache than TempJob
Persistent cannot be passed into a job — the safety system requires TempJob for all job data
Persistent is freed by the garbage collector, and big buffers cause GC pauses
cards.explain: You choose an allocator by lifetime: inside a job — Temp, one-off into a job — TempJob, long-lived — Persistent, allocated once. Memory access speed does not depend on the allocator; what differs is the cost of allocating and the checks.

wrong.1: Access is equally fast: Persistent is slow only at the moment of allocation.
wrong.2: It can be, and long-lived job buffers usually are Persistent.
wrong.3: The GC does not touch native memory at all — which is why you free it by hand.

lessons.title: Writing from a parallel job
lessons.sub: ParallelWriter with capacity up front, the queue, the hash map and NativeStream, two passes with a prefix sum

cards.title: Why you cannot just Add
cards.body:
In an IJobParallelFor the iterations run on different threads at the same time. That is why the safety system in the Editor lets Execute(i) write to a NativeArray only at its own index i; writing to another index throws. The [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction] attribute lifts that ban, but then guaranteeing there are no races is on you.

Often you do not know the size of the result in advance: out of 10,000 objects, say, 700 are visible.
