You cannot pack them densely “at your own index”, and a plain NativeList.Add from several threads is a race: two threads take the same slot, and growing the list reallocates the buffer while others are writing into it. Unity will not even schedule such a job: in the Editor Schedule() throws — the container does not support parallel writing.

cards.title: ParallelWriter and AddNoResize
cards.body:
Lists, queues and hash maps have a nested ParallelWriter type, which you get from AsParallelWriter(). The NativeList<T> writer can do one thing — AddNoResize: atomically take the next slot and write into it. It cannot grow: there is no safe way to reallocate a buffer while other threads are writing into it.

Hence the rule: capacity up front, at the upper bound. For a filter that is the input length. Overflowing it in the Editor throws InvalidOperationException; a regular build has no such checks, and the write goes past the end of the buffer.

And the second rule: the order is nondeterministic. Indices land in whatever order the threads got there, and it differs from run to run.

cards.q: Why does the list’s ParallelWriter have AddNoResize but no Add?
options: Growing means reallocating the buffer, and that cannot be done safely while other threads write into the same buffer
Add is slower, so it was removed for the sake of speed under Burst
Add exists, it just does not compile under Burst
In a parallel job the list length is fixed, so you cannot add at all
cards.explain: The writer only takes the next slot with an atomic counter. Memory cannot be reallocated while other threads write into it without a lock, so you set the capacity up front — at the upper bound of the result.

wrong.1: It is not about speed: there is simply no safe way to grow from several threads.
wrong.2: The list’s ParallelWriter has no Add method at all; Burst has nothing to do with it.
wrong.3: The length does grow — every AddNoResize increments it by 1. Only the capacity does not grow.

cards.task: Finish the visibility filter. In CullJob add a field visible of type NativeList<int>.ParallelWriter and in Execute append the index to it with AddNoResize. In ScheduleCull create the list with capacity positions.Length (Allocator.TempJob), give the job its AsParallelWriter() and schedule the job over positions.Length (second argument 64).

checks.label: CullJob has a NativeList<int>.ParallelWriter field
The index is appended with AddNoResize
There is no plain Add(...)
The list is created with a capacity and Allocator.TempJob
The job gets AsParallelWriter()
The job is scheduled over positions.Length

cards.explain: Capacity positions.Length is the upper bound: there cannot be more visible items than items. AddNoResize takes a slot atomically, so the threads do not get in each other’s way. The order of indices in visible changes from run to run — if it matters, sort afterwards or collect differently.

cards.title: NativeQueue and NativeParallelHashMap
cards.body:
NativeQueue<T> is a queue built from a chain of blocks. Its constructor takes no capacity: the AsParallelWriter() writer with its Enqueue(x) adds blocks by itself, so you do not have to work out the size in advance. You read it later on one thread with TryDequeue or ToArray. As with the list, the order across threads is not guaranteed.

NativeParallelHashMap<K,V> is a hash map with ParallelWriter.TryAdd(key, value), which returns false if the key is already there. You set the capacity up front — the parallel writer will not grow it. For several values per key there is NativeParallelMultiHashMap, the classic spatial hash: cell → indices of the objects in it.

A Collections 2.x trap: NativeHashMap is single-threaded and has no AsParallelWriter(). In Collections 2.1 the old map was renamed to NativeParallelHashMap, and the name NativeHashMap went to a new one — without parallel writing.
cards.code:
var events = new NativeQueue<DamageEvent>(Allocator.TempJob);   // grows by blocks
job.events = events.AsParallelWriter();                          // .Enqueue(e) in Execute

var grid = new NativeParallelMultiHashMap<int, int>(count, Allocator.TempJob); // capacity up front
hashJob.cells = grid.AsParallelWriter();                         // .Add(cell, i) in Execute

cards.title: NativeStream: a buffer per index and a stable order
cards.body:
NativeStream is a set of independent append-only buffers. You set the number of buffers when you create it; each buffer is written by one writer and read by one reader, with no synchronisation. A buffer grows in blocks without copying, so no capacity is needed up front.

In a parallel job you usually keep one buffer per iteration (or per batch of iterations): BeginForEachIndex(i), any number of Write calls, EndForEachIndex(). The reader then walks the buffers by index — and the result comes out in the same order on every run, however the threads were distributed. The price is one more step: read the stream and lay the result out (often the next job does it).

cards.title: Two passes: count → prefix sum → write
cards.body:
A technique from parallel algorithms that maps neatly onto jobs. When each element produces an unknown number of results and you need a dense array with a stable order:

  1. Count. A parallel job writes counts[i] — how many results element i will produce. That is a write at its own index, so the safety system’s restriction holds.
  2. Prefix sum. An IJob walks counts and writes offsets[i] — the sum of everything before it (an exclusive scan), and puts the grand total into a NativeReference.
  3. Write. A parallel job writes element i’s results into output starting at offsets[i]. The ranges do not overlap, but this is not “its own index”, so output needs [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction].

No atomics, a deterministic order, one dense array as the result. The price is two passes over the data and a scan on one thread; you allocate output at the upper bound.

cards.q: Put the steps of the two-pass write in order.
items: CountJob: each element writes counts[i] at its own index
ScanJob: offsets[i] is the sum of counts before i, total is the sum of all
WriteJob: element i writes its results into output starting at offsets[i]
Complete() the last job and read output from 0 to total
cards.explain: Each step depends on the previous one, so the three jobs form a chain through dependsOn, and Complete() is called once, at the end. The prefix sum turns “how many” into “where”, and the second parallel pass writes with no atomics and no races.

cards.q: Match the task with a way to collect results from a parallel job
pairs: Filter indices, the upper bound is known
Events with no upper bound, order does not matter
The same order on every run
NativeStream or two passes with a prefix sum

cards.q: What is true about writing from a parallel job? Select all.
options: If the capacity runs out, AddNoResize throws in the Editor
In Collections 2.x, NativeHashMap has AsParallelWriter()
NativeQueue.ParallelWriter does not need a preset capacity
The order of elements after AddNoResize is the same on every run
In the second pass of the prefix-sum scheme, output needs [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction]
cards.explain: Overflowing AddNoResize in the Editor throws InvalidOperationException; a build has no check. NativeHashMap in 2.x is single-threaded; for parallel writing use NativeParallelHashMap. The queue grows in blocks by itself. The ParallelWriter order depends on which thread got there first. In the second pass element i writes not at its own index but into its own range, so the restriction is lifted with the attribute.

cards.q: Interviewer: “You need a list of contacts from a parallel job, and in a replay it must match bit for bit. How do you collect it?”
options: NativeStream with a buffer per index, or two passes with a prefix sum: the element’s index decides the order, not whichever thread got there first
NativeList.ParallelWriter: AddNoResize is atomic, so the order is stable too
NativeQueue.ParallelWriter: a queue keeps the order of insertion
Any ParallelWriter: under Burst the threads always run in the same order
cards.explain: Atomicity protects against a race; it does not set the order. A stable order comes from schemes where the index determines where a result goes: NativeStream (read the buffers in order) or count → prefix sum → write. Another option is ParallelWriter plus a sort afterwards, but that is an extra O(n log n) pass.

wrong.1: The atomic counter guarantees that slots never collide, but who takes a slot first is up to the scheduler.
wrong.2: The queue hands elements out in insertion order, but with parallel writers that order itself depends on the threads and is not guaranteed.
wrong.3: Burst has no effect on how the scheduler hands iterations to threads.

lessons.title: batchSize
lessons.sub: What the second number in Schedule means, light work versus heavy, work stealing, and the Timeline instead of guessing

cards.title: batchSize — how many iterations per grab
cards.body:
Parallel scheduling takes two numbers: the length and the batchSize — the second argument of IJobParallelFor.Schedule(length, innerloopBatchCount, dependsOn) and IJobFor.ScheduleParallel(length, innerloopBatchCount, dependsOn). The range 0..length is cut into batches of batchSize iterations.

A thread takes a whole batch and runs its Execute calls back to back, in a tight inner loop. In the words of the docs, a value of 32 means the job queue steals 32 iterations and then performs them in an efficient inner loop.

A batch is indivisible: one thread runs it. So no more threads can work at once than there are batches.

cards.title: Work stealing
cards.body:
The batches are spread over several native jobs — roughly one per worker thread. Whoever finishes their own first steals from a neighbour: according to Unity’s docs, half of its remaining batches at a time, so that neighbouring data stays with one thread (cache locality).

Grabbing a batch is an atomic operation. So small batches balance the load better, but they are not free: every batch costs an atomic and a start of the inner loop.
flow: ran dry → steal half from a neighbour

cards.q: 1000 elements, batchSize 500, the machine has 8 worker threads. At most how many threads run this job at the same time?
cards.explain: 1000 / 500 = 2 batches. A whole batch runs on one thread, so at most two work in parallel and six sit idle, however many cores there are.

wrong.1: Eight threads could work if there were at least eight batches. There are two.
wrong.2: There would be one batch with a batchSize of 1000 or more.
wrong.3: batchSize is the batch size in iterations, not a thread count.

cards.title: Light work versus heavy work
cards.body:
Light work is a couple of multiplies and adds per element: move a particle, add two vectors. An iteration costs nanoseconds, comparable to grabbing a batch. Unity recommends 32–128. With a batchSize of 1, the overhead of grabbing every single iteration eats the gain.

Heavy work is pathfinding, tree traversal, hundreds of operations per element. Here the grab is cheap and the danger lies elsewhere: one big batch of expensive elements lands on a single thread and everyone waits for it — a long tail. Unity recommends a small batchSize, down to 1, especially when the cost per element is uneven.

And check the batch count: length / batchSize should be well above the number of worker threads, or some threads sit idle and stealing has nothing to share.
cards.deep: If you want to handle a batch yourself, Collections has IJobParallelForBatch: Execute(int startIndex, int count) receives the whole batch. Inside you can keep one scratch buffer per batch instead of one per element, or write a loop that is easier to optimise.

cards.q: Match the situation with the conclusion
pairs: 32–128: an iteration is cheaper than grabbing a batch
Pathfinding for 300 agents, costs vary a lot
One batch — one thread does the work
The grab overhead eats the gain

cards.title: The profiler instead of guessing
cards.body:
The numbers from the docs are a starting point, not the answer. The answer is in Profiler → CPU Usage → Timeline: it shows the worker threads and the slices named after your job.

  • A long tail: one or two threads are still computing, the rest are empty — the batches are too big, or the expensive elements ended up in one. Lower batchSize.
  • The job gets longer as you lower batchSize — the per-batch overhead now outweighs the work itself. Raise it.
  • WaitForJobGroupID on the main thread — the main thread is waiting for the job in Complete(). That is a signal not about batchSize but about collecting the result too early, or a job too long for the frame.

The method from the docs: start at 1 and increase until the gain becomes negligible. Measure on the target hardware, ideally in a development build: a phone and your workstation have different core counts.

cards.q: You are looking at the Timeline. What is true? Select all.
options: One thread computes the job for a long time while the others are empty — lower batchSize
WaitForJobGroupID on the main thread means the main thread is waiting for a job in Complete()
With 8 worker threads, batchSize should be length / 8
A good batchSize is the same on every device
If the job got longer when you lowered batchSize, the per-batch overhead won
cards.explain: A tail points to batches that are too big or uneven; time growing with small batches points to overhead. WaitForJobGroupID shows a wait in Complete(). One batch per thread leaves no slack for stealing: as soon as one thread is busy elsewhere or gets the expensive elements, everyone waits for it. Devices have different core counts, which is why batchSize is checked on the target hardware.

cards.task: In Crowd both jobs (IJobFor) are scheduled with a poor batchSize. MoveJob moves 100,000 particles — a couple of operations per element: use a value in the 32–128 range. PathJob finds a path for 200 agents and the cost varies a lot: use 1. Both jobs stay on ScheduleParallel; do not add Complete() to Update.

checks.label: MoveJob: batchSize from 32 to 128
PathJob: batchSize 1
There is no Complete() in Update
JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() is called after scheduling

cards.explain: With batchSize 1 the light MoveJob has 100,000 batches and as many grabs for next to no work. With 256, all 200 PathJob agents fall into one batch, and a single thread does all the pathfinding. After the fix, check the Timeline: MoveJob’s threads finish almost together, and PathJob has no lonely tail.

cards.q: Interviewer: “What batchSize do you usually use?”
options: It depends on the cost of an iteration: 32–128 for light work, down to 1 for heavy, uneven work. Then I check the Timeline on the target hardware
Always 64 — that is the value from the docs, so that is what people use
Always 1: that balances the load best
The element count divided by the core count — exactly one batch per thread
cards.explain: A good answer names both ends, explains why (grab overhead versus the tail) and ends with a measurement. “I tune batchSize from the Timeline” sounds like experience; a single number sounds memorised.

wrong.1: 64 is a reasonable start for light work, but pathfinding for 200 agents is then only four batches: at most four threads work, and one expensive batch makes a tail.
wrong.2: On light work, batchSize 1 spends more on grabbing batches than on the work itself.
wrong.3: One batch per thread leaves no slack for stealing: one expensive chunk or one busy thread and everyone waits.

lessons.title: Final: data, safety and dependencies
lessons.sub: The struct copy, the safety system, job chains, allocators, parallel writing and batchSize — questions, two coding tasks and practice in Unity

cards.q: A job accumulates a total in the field sum. After Complete() the main thread reads job.sum and sees 0. Why?
options: The job received a copy of the struct, and the sum was computed in the copy. Results come back only through a container, such as NativeReference<float>
Burst does not support float fields in jobs and silently zeroes them
Complete() did not wait for the job to finish; you need to check IsCompleted
The sum field must be marked [WriteOnly], then the value comes back
cards.explain: Schedule() copies the job struct, and Execute works on the copy. Plain fields are inputs; they never travel back. The result gets out only through a native container, because a copy of the struct points to the same memory. For a single value, use NativeReference<T>.

wrong.1: float is the most ordinary blittable type; Burst handles it fine.
wrong.2: Complete() does wait for the job. The issue is not timing but that the work happened in a copy.
wrong.3: [WriteOnly] applies to containers and restricts access; it does not return field values.

cards.q: What is true about the safety system? Select all.
options: In the Editor, two independent jobs writing to one NativeArray cause an exception when the second is scheduled
In a player build the same checks catch the race and log an error
[ReadOnly] lets two jobs read the same container at the same time
A disabling attribute such as [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction] lifts the check, and guaranteeing there are no races is on you
If the safety system stays silent in the Editor, the code certainly has no race
cards.explain: In the Editor the safety system knows who reads and writes each container and throws on a conflict without a dependency. In a player build those checks are unavailable, so a race there is silent data corruption. [ReadOnly] allows parallel reads. Disabling attributes switch the check off entirely: past that line the safety system sees nothing, so its silence proves no absence of races.

cards.q: Lay out a crowd physics frame: a chain of jobs from positions to transforms.
items: Positions job: integrate velocities
Spatial hash: NativeParallelMultiHashMap.ParallelWriter buckets objects into cells
Collisions: read your own cell and its neighbours, write contacts
Transforms: write the new positions into each Transform
Complete() the last JobHandle — once, when the result is needed
cards.explain: Each link gets the previous link’s JobHandle through dependsOn, and the whole chain runs on worker threads while the main thread does its own work. The hash is built from the new positions, and collisions read the finished hash. Complete() comes only at the end: completing the last link completes all the earlier ones.

cards.q: Trap: which line takes away the chain’s parallelism with the main thread?
cards.explain: hash.Complete() in the middle of the chain: the main thread waits for two jobs even though the next links would get the dependency through hash anyway. Delete that line — the dependency is already passed as the third argument to Schedule, and the result can be collected in LateUpdate through handle.

cards.task: Radar: CullJob (an IJobParallelFor with a NativeList<int>.ParallelWriter) selects the visible points, SumJob (an IJob) adds up their weights into NativeReference<float> total. In Update, schedule cull over positions.Length (second argument 64), then sum depending on cull, and store sum’s handle in the field handle. Wake the worker threads. Complete() and reading total.Value go in LateUpdate.

checks.label: CullJob is scheduled over positions.Length
SumJob is scheduled with a dependency, and its JobHandle is stored in the field handle
Update calls JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs()
There is no Complete() in Update
LateUpdate calls Complete(), then reads total.Value

cards.explain: All buffers are Persistent and reused; Clear() resets the list length without reallocating. SumJob reads visible only after the cull — the dependency guarantees it, not a Complete(). Completing the last handle in LateUpdate completes the whole chain, and until then the main thread is free.

cards.q: In code review: the positions buffer is created every frame with new NativeArray(..., Allocator.Persistent) and freed in LateUpdate. It works. What do you say?
options: The buffer is needed every frame — allocate it as Persistent once in Awake, reuse it, and free it in OnDestroy after Complete(). Persistent every frame is the slowest allocation with no lifetime checks
Switch to Allocator.Temp — it is the fastest and needs no Dispose
It is all fine: Persistent is more reliable than TempJob, leave it
Drop the Dispose: Persistent frees itself when you exit Play Mode
cards.explain: You pick an allocator by lifetime. Data needed every frame is long-lived: one Persistent allocation and one free. A one-off buffer into a job is TempJob; scratch data inside a job is Temp.

wrong.1: Main-thread Temp cannot be passed into a job: in the Editor Schedule() throws an exception.
wrong.2: It works, but it pays for the most expensive allocation every frame, and nobody catches a forgotten Dispose after 4 frames here.
wrong.3: Persistent lives until Dispose: without it you get a leak, which leak detection will report.

cards.q: Match each container with how it writes from a parallel job
pairs: Enqueue, grows in blocks by itself
TryAdd, false on a repeated key
A buffer per index, a stable order

cards.q: An IJobFor over 300 agents, ScheduleParallel(agents.Length, 512, default). In the Timeline a single thread computes the whole job. Why, and what do you do?
options: 300 is less than 512 — that makes one batch, and one thread runs a batch. The work is heavy, so batchSize 1 and a check in the Timeline
ScheduleParallel always runs on one thread; you need Schedule
There are too few worker threads: on a machine with more cores the job will spread out by itself
Call Complete() earlier so the main thread helps
cards.explain: A batch is indivisible, and the batch count is length / batchSize rounded up — one here. For heavy, uneven work batchSize is kept small, down to 1, and then you check whether the tail is gone.

wrong.1: The other way round: ScheduleParallel is the parallel variant, while IJobFor’s Schedule runs everything on one worker thread.
wrong.2: However many cores there are, there is one batch — and one thread will run it.
wrong.3: Completing earlier only makes the main thread wait; there is still one batch.

cards.task: ScheduleHeat schedules two jobs and waits right away. Fix it: BlurJob reads tmp, which SampleJob writes — schedule it with a dependency on the first job (the third argument to Schedule). Remove every Complete(): the method returns a JobHandle that will be completed later. Free tmp without waiting via tmp.Dispose(handle) and return the handle it gives back.

checks.label: BlurJob is scheduled with a dependency on SampleJob
There is no Complete()
tmp is freed with Dispose(JobHandle)
There is no tmp.Dispose() without an argument
The method returns the JobHandle that tmp.Dispose(...) returned

cards.explain: The original has two bugs at once: without a dependency BlurJob reads tmp while SampleJob writes it (an exception at scheduling in the Editor, a race in a build), and Complete() plus an immediate Dispose() kill the parallelism. With the dependency and Dispose(JobHandle), the whole “sample → blur → free” chain runs on worker threads, and the caller collects it with a single Complete().

cards.q: Trap. A colleague on Collections 2.x writes: var map = new NativeHashMap<int, int>(n, Allocator.TempJob); job.map = map.AsParallelWriter(); What happens?
options: It does not compile: in Collections 2.x NativeHashMap has no AsParallelWriter. For parallel writing use NativeParallelHashMap
It works, but the key order is nondeterministic
It works only without Burst
It compiles, but the safety system throws when the job is scheduled
cards.explain: In Collections 2.1 the old map with parallel writing became NativeParallelHashMap, and NativeHashMap is now single-threaded with no parallel writer. Code from older tutorials does not build on 2.x — a common lead-in to “which version did you work with?”.

wrong.1: It never gets as far as ordering: NativeHashMap in 2.x has no AsParallelWriter method.
wrong.2: Burst has nothing to do with it: the method is not in the API.
wrong.3: The error comes earlier — at compile time.

cards.q: You are asked to explain out loud: “Why does a race throw an exception in the Editor but not in a build?” Put the answer in order.
items: In the Editor every native container has a safety system handle: Unity knows which jobs read and write it
Scheduling a job that conflicts with an unfinished one, without a dependency, throws
These checks exist only in the Editor: in a player build they are unavailable, not merely switched off
So in a build the same race is silent data corruption or a crash, not an error in the log
Takeaway: I catch races in the Editor, and in a build correctness comes from dependencies, not from checks
cards.explain: Mechanism → rule → cost: who keeps track (the safety system handle), when it fires (a conflict without a dependency), why a build is silent (there are no checks) and what that means for your work.

cards.title: Practice in Unity
cards.body:
A 45–60 minute task. Unity 6 with the Burst, Collections and Mathematics packages. A radar over 50,000 points.

  1. Make a MonoBehaviour with Persistent buffers: 50,000 float3 positions (random in a 500 m cube), weights, a NativeList<int> visible with capacity equal to the point count, and a NativeReference<float>. Allocate them in Awake, free them in OnDestroy after Complete().
  2. Every frame: MoveJob (IJobFor, ScheduleParallel) moves the points, CullJob with a ParallelWriter selects points within a radius of the camera, SumJob (IJob) adds up the weights. Chain them through dependsOn, call JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() after scheduling, and Complete() in LateUpdate.
  3. Write a second version of the filter with two passes — counts → ScanJob → WriteJob — and a switch between the two.
  4. Run MoveJob and CullJob with batchSize 1, 8, 64, 512 and 8192.

What to measure.

  • Profiler → Timeline: the jobs run on worker threads during the other Update calls; check for WaitForJobGroupID in LateUpdate; see how the picture changes with batchSize — a tail at 8192, longer times at 1.
  • With the camera still, compare the first indices in visible across two frames: with ParallelWriter the order changes, with the two-pass version it does not.
  • Temporarily remove the Dispose() from OnDestroy, set Leak Detection Level to EnabledWithStackTrace and wait for a domain unload (for example, a script recompile): the console shows a leak report with the allocation stack. Put the Dispose() back.
  • Temporarily drop SumJob’s dependency: in the Editor you should get a safety system exception at scheduling.

You are done when the main thread barely waits in LateUpdate; the console shows no leaks and no exceptions; the weight sums of the two filter versions match; and you can name the batchSize after which the time stops dropping, and explain why.

units.title: Deeper: how Burst makes code fast
units.blurb: Vectorization and the Burst Inspector, SoA versus AoS, float determinism, debugging Burst, FunctionPointer and SharedStatic, transforms and physics from jobs, and when Burst is not worth it.

lessons.title: Vectorization
lessons.sub: How Burst handles 4–8 numbers with one instruction, and what gets in its way

cards.title: SIMD: one instruction, several numbers
cards.body:
The main reason Burst is fast on number crunching is SIMD (single instruction, multiple data). A CPU register holds several numbers instead of one, and a single instruction processes all of them at once.

SSE has 128-bit xmm registers, which is 4 floats. AVX/AVX2 has 256-bit ymm registers, 8 floats. ARM has NEON, 128 bits. The instruction sets to build for are chosen in the Burst AOT settings; if you pick several, Burst puts several variants of the code into the build and picks the one that fits the CPU at startup.

The usual road to SIMD is loop auto-vectorization: LLVM takes several iterations and turns them into one instruction. You write a plain for, and the assembly shows a vmulps doing 8 numbers. The same holds inside IJobParallelFor and IJobFor with ScheduleParallel: Execute is inlined into the loop each worker runs over its batch of indices, and Burst can vectorize that loop. But only if the body meets the conditions.

cards.title: When a loop vectorizes
cards.body:
The compiler merges iterations only if that doesn’t change the result. Hence the conditions:

Iterations are independent. a[i] = a[i - 1] * 0.5f can’t be merged: every step waits for the previous one.

The trip count is known on entry. A break or return in the middle, and in the Burst manual’s example the loop turns scalar.

Memory is contiguous. a[i], a[i + 1]… load with one instruction. If the fields are scattered across structs, the numbers have to be gathered one by one (that’s the SoA lesson).

Writes don’t overlap reads — that’s aliasing, next card.

A float sum is a dependency too. Vectorizing it means reordering the additions, and with the default FloatMode (Strict) Burst doesn’t do that. More in the determinism lesson.

cards.q: Which loop in a Burst job vectorizes (fields are NativeArray<float>, default FloatMode)?
options: for (i…) output[i] = math.sqrt(a[i]) * k;
for (i…) { if (a[i] == target) { found = i; break; } }
for (i…) total += a[i];   // total is a float
cards.explain: The iterations are independent, the memory is contiguous and there is no early exit, so the square root and the multiply become sqrtps and mulps on several numbers at a time. break makes the trip count unknown, a[i - 1] depends on the previous step, and a float sum needs the additions reordered, which Strict doesn’t allow.

wrong.1: A break in the middle: the compiler doesn’t know how many iterations will run, so the loop stays scalar.
wrong.2: Each iteration reads what the previous one wrote. That’s a prefix sum, and it can’t be merged into one instruction.
wrong.3: A vector sum is 8 partial sums added up at the end, which is a different order of additions. In Strict mode Burst doesn’t change the order.

cards.title: Aliasing and [NoAlias]
cards.body:
Aliasing is when two pointers look at overlapping memory. If dst may equal src + 1, writing dst[i] changes src[i + 1], and processing 8 elements at once is no longer valid. A compiler that isn’t sure has to go one by one, or insert an overlap check before the loop.

In a job this is solved for you: the job struct and its container fields (NativeArray, NativeSlice) are treated as non-overlapping by default. That is why a plain loop in a job vectorizes “for free”. The exception is a field marked [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction]: Burst assumes it may overlap the others.

In a static method on pointers you make the promise yourself: [NoAlias] on a parameter means “doesn’t overlap the other parameters”. Nobody checks the promise: if the memory does overlap, you get undefined behaviour and very nasty bugs. Different element types don’t save you from aliasing either: in C#, Burst draws no such conclusion.

cards.q: What is true about aliasing in Burst? Pick all that apply.
options: NativeArray fields of a job struct are treated as non-overlapping by default
Burst treats a field marked [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction] as possibly overlapping the others
If you put [NoAlias] on pointers that actually overlap, Burst detects it and throws an exception
A NativeArray<byte> and a NativeArray<float> can’t overlap because their types differ
cards.explain: Burst treats the containers of a job as non-overlapping by default — that’s why loops in jobs vectorize so well. [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction] removes that guarantee too. [NoAlias] is a promise, not a check: a false promise is undefined behaviour. And Burst doesn’t reason “different types, different memory”: in C# a byte pointer can point where a float pointer does.

cards.title: Branch → math.select
cards.body:
A SIMD instruction takes 8 numbers down one path. If each element has its own if, the 8 “lanes” may want different paths, and you can’t jump. The compiler has to turn the branch into a masked choice or leave the loop scalar. LLVM rewrites simple cases on its own, but not always: a write inside the branch, a long body, a call — and there’s no vectorization.

math.select(a, b, c) from Unity.Mathematics makes the choice explicit: it returns b if c is true, otherwise a. Both sides are computed up front and a mask picks one — no jump. There are overloads for float4 with bool4, where the choice is made per lane.

The price is that both sides get computed. For cheap expressions that’s nothing; for heavy ones (a call, a loop) it isn’t. For the common cases there are ready-made branch-free functions: math.min, math.max, math.clamp, math.abs.

cards.q: Build the line without a branch: if the speed is above maxSpeed, take maxSpeed, otherwise the speed itself.
cards.explain: math.select(ifFalse, ifTrue, condition): when s > maxSpeed it returns the second argument, maxSpeed, otherwise the first, s. The short way to write the same thing is math.min(s, maxSpeed).

cards.title: Burst Inspector: mulss vs mulps
cards.body:
Whether a loop vectorized is not something you guess — you look. Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector, pick the job under Compile Targets on the left, and the Assembly view on the right.

You don’t need to read all of it. Find the body of the hot loop and look at the instruction suffix: ss is scalar single, one number (mulss, addss); ps is packed single, the whole register (mulps, addps). The v prefix is just the AVX encoding: vmulss is still one number. ymm registers hold 8 floats, xmm hold 4 or one.

The Highlight SIMD Scalar vs Packed option helps: it colours scalar and packed instructions differently. If the loop didn’t vectorize, the LLVM IR Optimization Diagnostics view tells you what got in the way.

There is also a compile-time check: Loop.ExpectVectorized() from Unity.Burst.CompilerServices gives error BC1321 if the loop isn’t vectorized. It is experimental — it needs the UNITY_BURST_EXPERIMENTAL_LOOP_INTRINSICS define — and it doesn’t work inside an if.

cards.q: In the Burst Inspector the body of the hot loop looks like this. What does it mean?
cards.code:
.LBB0_4:
    vmovss  xmm1, dword ptr [rdx + 4*rax]
    vmulss  xmm1, xmm1, dword ptr [r8 + 4*rax]
    vmovss  dword ptr [rcx + 4*rax], xmm1
    inc     rax
    cmp     rax, r9
    jl      .LBB0_4
options: The loop isn’t vectorized: vmulss multiplies one number per iteration, even though it’s an AVX-encoded instruction
The loop is vectorized for AVX: the v prefix and xmm registers mean 4 numbers at a time
Burst is off, and this is Mono code
Safety checks are on; without them the code would be packed
cards.explain: The ss suffix is scalar single: one number. The v prefix is only the AVX encoding, and xmm is used for a single lane here. On every iteration rax grows by 1 — one element. Next stop: LLVM IR Optimization Diagnostics, to see what got in the way, aliasing or a branch.

wrong.1: The vector version would be vmulps (packed), and the counter would grow by 4 or 8. Here it’s ss and inc rax.
wrong.2: The Inspector’s Assembly view shows the code Burst compiled, not Mono.
wrong.3: Checks add comparisons and calls, but the ss suffix is about a scalar instruction, not about checks.

cards.task: Remove the branch from DamageJob: Execute must compute the result with math.select (add Unity.Mathematics), with no if. If the damage is greater than or equal to the health, the result is 0, otherwise hp − damage. Keep the [BurstCompile] attribute.

checks.label: using Unity.Mathematics is added
Execute contains math.select
Execute has no if
The result is written to result[i]
DamageJob still has [BurstCompile]

cards.explain: Both sides — 0 and hp − damage — are cheap, so computing both and picking with a mask beats a jump: the IJobFor loop stays vectorizable. math.max(0f, hp[i] - damage[i]) would work here too. In the interview: “I take branches out of the hot loop with math.select or min/max and check in the Burst Inspector that the instructions are packed.”

cards.q: Interviewer: “The same loop vectorizes in a job over NativeArray, but not in a static Burst method on pointers. Why, and what do you do?”
options: Burst doesn’t know that dst and src don’t overlap; I promise it with [NoAlias] on the parameters and check in the Inspector
Burst never vectorizes static methods, so I move the code into a job
The k parameter is the problem; it should be a field
Pointers are banned in Burst, so I replace them with NativeArray
cards.explain: A job’s container fields are NoAlias by default, but the compiler knows nothing about two raw pointers: dst may equal src + 1. All it can do is go one by one or check for overlap on entry. [NoAlias] settles the question — provided you really guarantee the memory doesn’t overlap.

wrong.1: Static [BurstCompile] methods are compiled by the same Burst and vectorize by the same rules.
wrong.2: The scalar k is the same for every iteration and gets in nobody’s way.
wrong.3: Pointers and unsafe code are allowed in Burst.

lessons.title: SoA vs AoS
lessons.sub: Why memory layout matters more than it seems, and how Entities is built around it

cards.title: Memory arrives in cache lines
cards.body:
A CPU doesn’t read one number from memory. It reads a cache line — 64 bytes on most modern CPUs (128 on Apple Silicon). Read one float, and its 15 neighbours land in L1 too.

A miss that goes all the way to RAM costs on the order of a hundred nanoseconds — hundreds of cycles in which SIMD code could have processed thousands of numbers. So in number crunching the speed is set not by the arithmetic but by how many useful bytes each line brings in.

The other ally is the prefetcher: on a sequential walk it loads the next lines ahead of time, and there are almost no misses. With random access by index it can’t help.

Hence the rule: the data a hot loop reads together should sit contiguous and dense, with no unrelated fields in between.

cards.title: AoS: array of structures
cards.body:
AoS (array of structures) is the familiar layout: a Unit struct with all its fields and a NativeArray<Unit>. The fields of one unit sit together, the units follow one another.

The movement loop reads the position and the velocity — 24 bytes — but a unit takes 52, and all 52 pass through the cache. More than half of every line is rotation, health and team, which this loop doesn’t need. Add more fields to Unit, and the loop gets slower even though its code didn’t change.

Vectorization suffers too. The x coordinates of neighbouring units are 52 bytes apart, so one instruction can’t load them: the compiler has to gather the numbers one by one or leave the code scalar.

AoS is good when an object is accessed as a whole and in random order: read one unit, and all its fields are in one or two lines.

cards.title: SoA: structure of arrays
cards.body:
SoA (structure of arrays) puts each field in its own array: positions, velocities, health… Element i is index i in all of them.

The movement loop now reads only two arrays, and every byte of every cache line is useful. The prefetcher follows two sequential streams, and neighbouring elements of one field sit side by side — exactly what SIMD needs.

NativeArray<float3> is a compromise: inside a float3, x, y and z are still together. For operations that treat all components the same way (pos += vel * dt) that hardly matters. If the formula mixes components (a length, a dot product), the fully split px, py, pz layout gives the compiler the easiest case: 8 x values in one ymm load.

cards.q: A pos += vel * dt loop over 100,000 units. Why is SoA faster than AoS?
options: Only positions and velocities reach the cache, and neighbouring elements of one field are contiguous: full cache lines and SIMD
There are more arrays, and the Job System hands them to different worker threads
SoA takes less memory than AoS
Burst can’t handle structs inside a NativeArray
cards.explain: The byte count is the same, but the loop touches only what it needs: 24 bytes per unit instead of 52, and the lines are filled with useful data. On top of that, neighbouring values of one field load with a single SIMD instruction.

wrong.1: Threads split the indices, not the arrays: in AoS and SoA alike each thread takes its own batch of i.
wrong.2: The total amount of data is the same — the same fields, just laid out differently.
wrong.3: Structs in a NativeArray are normal for Burst; the only question is how many wasted bytes go through the cache.

cards.title: Lay out by access, not by class
cards.body:
SoA doesn’t mean “every field separate at any cost”. Group fields by who reads them and how often: hot (position and velocity — movement and collisions every frame), warm (health and cooldown — AI a few times a second), cold (the name — UI and save games). This is called a hot/cold split.

The price of SoA: more arrays, which have to be passed to the job together; removing an element means RemoveAtSwapBack in every array, or the indices drift apart; the code reads worse than unit.health. And reading all the fields of one object touches several lines in different arrays — for random access to a single unit, AoS can be faster.

The rule: pick the layout for the hot loops. If a loop over 100,000 elements reads 2 fields out of 10, go SoA. If the code takes one object and reads everything, stay AoS.

cards.q: What do you pay for SoA? Pick all that apply.
options: Removing an element has to be repeated in every array, or the indices drift apart
Reading all the fields of one object touches several cache lines in different arrays
The Job System can’t split a job with several arrays into batches
SoA is always slower than AoS if the loop reads more than one field
cards.explain: Keeping the indices in sync is your job: forget RemoveAtSwapBack in one array, and a unit gets someone else’s velocity. And random access to one object in SoA is smeared across several lines. The Job System splits index batches the same way whatever the number of arrays, and a loop that reads two or three fields out of many is exactly where SoA wins.

cards.title: Entities: chunks by component type
cards.body:
Entities is SoA out of the box. The set of component types of an entity is its archetype. Entities of one archetype live in 16 KiB chunks, and inside a chunk each component type has its own dense array, plus an array of the entity ids themselves.

A system that reads LocalTransform and Velocity walks exactly two arrays in each chunk and doesn’t pull health, AI or any other component into the cache. It’s the same SoA, just by component rather than by single field. Removing an entity moves the chunk’s last element into the freed slot — the same swap-back.

Inside a component it’s AoS: the fields of one struct sit together. That’s why components are kept small and split by access: what’s read together goes into one component, what’s rarely needed into another.

In the interview: “Entities stores components by type in chunks, so a job reads only the arrays it needs, contiguously, and Burst vectorizes it.”

cards.q: Match the layout to how the data sits
pairs: All fields of one object together
One field of all objects in a row
An array per component type inside 16 KiB
Frequent fields apart from rare ones

cards.task: Move MoveJob from AoS to SoA: instead of NativeArray<Boid>, two fields — NativeArray<float3> positions (read and written) and NativeArray<float3> velocities with [ReadOnly]. In Execute, move positions[i] by velocities[i] * dt. Keep the [BurstCompile] attribute.

checks.label: There is a NativeArray<float3> positions field
There is a NativeArray<float3> velocities field with [ReadOnly]
The job has no NativeArray<Boid>
Execute increases positions[i] by velocities[i] * dt
MoveJob still has [BurstCompile]

cards.explain: A Boid takes 44 bytes, and movement needs 24: after the split only positions and velocities go through the cache, while colour and flock stay in their own arrays. [ReadOnly] on velocities tells the safety system that other jobs may read the array in parallel. In the interview: “SoA so the compiler can vectorize — I check the Burst Inspector.”

cards.q: A 64-byte component was added to the unit archetype. The movement system reads only LocalTransform and Velocity. What changes for it?
options: It reads the same arrays, but fewer entities fit into a 16 KiB chunk — more chunks, more per-chunk overhead
It becomes about twice as slow: the new component goes through the cache too
Nothing changes at all
A structural change happens every frame
cards.explain: The useful bytes are the same: the LocalTransform and Velocity arrays are dense, other components sit in their own arrays and stay out of the cache. But a fixed-size chunk is shared by all the archetype’s components, so there are fewer entities per chunk and more chunks. Usually a small cost, but heavy, rarely used data gets moved out of the hot archetype.

wrong.1: Components sit in the chunk as separate arrays; the system never touches the new component’s array.
wrong.2: The chunk capacity went down, so there are more chunks — there is a little overhead.
wrong.3: A structural change is adding a component to an entity, not reading. The archetype here is already like that.

cards.q: Interviewer: “A NativeArray<Enemy> with 20 fields, and a job that only moves positions every frame. What do you suggest, and how do you check it?”
options: Move positions and velocities into separate arrays (a hot/cold split), compare the job time in the Profiler, and check in the Burst Inspector whether the instructions turned packed
Increase batchSize so each thread takes more enemies
Make Enemy a class so the 20 fields aren’t copied
Put [NoAlias] on the enemy array
cards.explain: The problem is bytes: the loop drags 20 fields through the cache for the sake of two. Splitting by access fixes it, and the Profiler and the Burst Inspector confirm it: the job time drops, and the loop body shows ps instructions instead of ss.

wrong.1: batchSize changes how work is spread across threads, not how many wasted bytes each element carries.
wrong.2: Classes aren’t allowed in Burst, and an array of references would also scatter the objects across the heap.
wrong.3: A job’s container fields are already treated as non-overlapping; aliasing has nothing to do with it.

lessons.title: Determinism and float
lessons.sub: FloatMode, FloatPrecision, FMA, and what is actually guaranteed when two clients must compute the same thing

cards.title: The order of operations changes the result
cards.body:
float addition isn’t associative: (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can differ in the last bits, and sometimes by a lot. In the example, 1e8f + 1f rounds back to 1e8f and the one is lost — in the other order it survives.

Hence the sources of divergence that come up in interviews:

Reordering. A vectorized sum is 8 partial sums added at the end, which is a different order.

FMA — multiply and add in one instruction, with one rounding instead of two.

Different function implementations: sin, exp and pow are approximated differently in different libraries and instruction sets.

For graphics this doesn’t matter. It matters where two machines must get the same bits: a lockstep multiplayer game, input-based replays, anti-cheat by recomputation.

cards.title: FMA: more accurate, but different
cards.body:
FMA (fused multiply-add) computes a * b + c in one instruction and rounds once. That is more accurate than multiplying, rounding, adding and rounding again. But the bits come out different.

So FMA is a problem of agreement, not accuracy: if one machine’s compiler fused the operation and another’s didn’t (another CPU, another code variant, another mode), the results diverge. Over thousands of simulation steps, a difference in the last bit turns into a unit standing somewhere else.

In Burst, fusing into FMA is allowed by FloatMode.Fast. Unity.Mathematics has math.mad(a, b, c), and its documentation says outright that with fast math on some architectures it may become an FMA.

cards.title: FloatMode: Strict, Fast, Deterministic
cards.body:
FloatMode is set in [BurstCompile] and says what liberties with float the compiler may take.

Default is the same as Strict: no reordering, denormals and NaN are respected.

Fast allows algebraically equivalent reordering, multiplying by a reciprocal instead of dividing, and FMA; the compiler may assume there are no NaNs or infinities. Faster, but the result may differ from Strict.

Deterministic gives the same result on all supported platforms. It works since Burst 1.8.25; before that the value was reserved and did nothing. 64-bit architectures only. Burst turns off the optimizations that cause platform differences and flushes subnormals to zero everywhere; identical NaN bits are not promised, and speed may drop.

The mode can be set per job, for a whole assembly with [assembly: BurstCompile(...)], and the Burst AOT settings have a default Floating Point Mode.

cards.q: A job that sums forces was given FloatMode.Fast. The result now differs from before in the last digits. What is it?
options: Expected behaviour: Fast allows reordering and fusing into FMA, hence different last bits
A Burst bug — roll back the package version
A data race between worker threads
In Fast mode Burst computes in half instead of float
cards.explain: Fast changes the order of the computation and may fuse a multiply with an add — mathematically the same result, but different bits. If the bits themselves matter, you don’t use Fast.

wrong.1: This is the documented behaviour of the mode, not a compiler bug.
wrong.2: A race would give results that jump around, not consistently different ones; besides, the float mode has nothing to do with threads.
wrong.3: Fast doesn’t change the type: a float stays 32-bit. What changes is the order of operations and how they’re fused.

cards.title: FloatPrecision: function accuracy
cards.body:
FloatPrecision is a separate knob: how accurately Burst computes math.sin, math.cos, math.exp, math.log, math.pow and the like. Accuracy is measured in ulp (unit in the last place) — the distance between neighbouring floats of that magnitude.

Standard is the default and the same as Medium: 3.5 ulp. High is 1 ulp. Low is up to 350 ulp for sin, cos, exp, log, pow, fmod and their variants; other functions are as in Medium.

Don’t mix them up: FloatPrecision is about accuracy, FloatMode is about freedom to reorder and agreement of results. High doesn’t make code deterministic, and Low is a fair choice for waves, particles and other effects where nobody will see an error in the third digit.

cards.q: Match the setting to what it does
pairs: No reordering; NaN and denormals respected
The same result on all 64-bit platforms
sin, exp, pow with an error of up to 350 ulp

cards.title: What is guaranteed and what isn’t
cards.body:
Essentially one thing is guaranteed: the same code, the same inputs, the same order, the same build on the same CPU — the same bits from run to run.

Not promised in Strict or Fast: the same result on x64 and ARM64; on two x64 machines, if Burst picked different code variants for them (SSE4 and AVX2); between Burst and Mono/IL2CPP for the same formula.

Deterministic covers platforms, but only for Burst code. If the float inputs came from managed code, or Burst calls a function pointer compiled without Deterministic, the guarantee breaks.

The order is your job in any mode. If a parallel job writes into a queue through a ParallelWriter, the element order depends on which thread got there first — and a sum in another order is another sum. For determinism, the data is sorted or written to fixed indices, and summed in one order.

cards.q: A lockstep game with the simulation in Burst. What can make two clients diverge? Pick all that apply.
options: FloatMode.Fast on the simulation job
A float sum over elements a parallel job wrote through a ParallelWriter, in arrival order
Part of a formula computed in a MonoBehaviour and part in Burst, with clients on different platforms
Integer arithmetic in a fixed order
FloatMode.Deterministic on 64-bit clients with the same inputs and order
cards.explain: Fast reorders and fuses into FMA differently on different machines. The arrival order from a ParallelWriter changes from run to run, and the float sum changes with it. Deterministic doesn’t cover managed code, and its floats on different platforms don’t have to agree. Integers in a fixed order agree everywhere, and Deterministic with the same inputs and order is exactly the case the mode was made for.

cards.title: Fixed point for lockstep
cards.body:
The classic answer for lockstep is fixed point: a number is stored as an integer multiplied by a constant factor. In 16.16 format the value 1.5 is stored as 98304 (1.5 × 65536). Addition is an integer add, multiplication goes through a long and a shift.

Integer arithmetic gives the same bits everywhere: on x64 and ARM, in 32 and 64 bits, in Burst and in Mono. That’s why many lockstep RTS games are built this way.

The price: a narrow range (16.16 is about ±32,768) and overflow you have to keep in mind; your own sqrt, sin and tables; longer code that is slower to write. And everything Unity computes for you in float (physics, animation) can’t be part of the simulation.

FloatMode.Deterministic is a newer alternative if all clients are 64-bit and the whole simulation runs in Burst.

cards.q: A lockstep RTS: clients on Windows x64, Android ARM64 and old 32-bit Android. The simulation is in Burst. What do you pick for the simulation numbers?
options: Fixed point on integers: the same bits on every client, 32-bit ones included
FloatMode.Deterministic for the whole assembly
FloatMode.Strict: it reorders nothing, so the results will match
FloatPrecision.High: at 1 ulp there will be no divergence
cards.explain: Deterministic is supported only on 64-bit architectures, and the list has 32-bit clients. Strict doesn’t reorder operations, but doesn’t promise agreement across platforms. That leaves integers.

wrong.1: Deterministic is 64-bit only. The 32-bit Android clients aren’t covered.
wrong.2: Strict removes reordering, but not the differences between platforms and function implementations.
wrong.3: FloatPrecision is about function accuracy, not agreement: a 1 ulp error that differs between machines is already a divergence.

cards.task: Set the modes. ParticleJob is visual sparks: give it FloatMode.Fast and FloatPrecision.Low. SimStepJob is a lockstep simulation step, and all clients are 64-bit: give it FloatMode.Deterministic. No bare [BurstCompile] without parameters may remain.

checks.label: ParticleJob has FloatMode.Fast in [BurstCompile]
ParticleJob has FloatPrecision.Low in [BurstCompile]
SimStepJob has FloatMode.Deterministic in [BurstCompile]
Neither job is left with a parameterless [BurstCompile]

cards.explain: Nobody compares sparks bit by bit, so they may have both reordering and rough functions. The simulation must agree on every client, so it gets Deterministic (Burst 1.8.25+, 64-bit), and the inputs and processing order must be the same everywhere. Both ways of writing it, the constructor (FloatPrecision.Low, FloatMode.Fast) and FloatMode = ..., are equally valid.

cards.q: Interviewer: “Why not just turn on FloatMode.Deterministic for the whole assembly, to be safe?”
options: It turns off some float optimizations and can slow the code down; it’s only needed where results must agree between machines
Because Deterministic is reserved and does nothing
It doesn’t work with IJobParallelFor
It requires FloatPrecision.Low
cards.explain: Determinism is paid for in speed: Burst gives up the optimizations that cause platform differences. It’s enabled selectively — for the simulation, replays, server-side verification — while rendering, particles and animation stay on Default or Fast.

wrong.1: That was true before Burst 1.8.25. Since that version Deterministic is supported (on 64-bit platforms).
wrong.2: The float mode applies to the compiled code and doesn’t depend on the job type.
wrong.3: FloatPrecision and FloatMode are independent.

lessons.title: How to debug Burst
lessons.sub: Is the bug in the logic, the threads or Burst; how to set a breakpoint, what to log, and how to measure speed

cards.title: First find out whether it’s Burst
cards.body:
Debugging a Burst job is two different tasks: a wrong result and too slow. Let’s start with the first.

The first question is whether Burst or your logic is to blame. Turn off Jobs > Burst > Enable Compilation: jobs run as plain C#, and the usual managed breakpoints work. The bug is still there — it’s in the logic, hunt it down the usual way. It’s gone — look at what behaves differently under Burst: a false [NoAlias], fields with [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction], FloatMode.Fast.

You don’t always have to turn everything off: put a managed breakpoint into Burst code with a debugger attached, and Unity disables Burst for that code path by itself, and turns it back on once you remove the breakpoints.

A trap: in the Editor Burst compiles in the background, and the first frames may run managed code. For a Burst-vs-managed comparison and for measurements, wait for the compilation: [BurstCompile(CompileSynchronously = true)] on the job or Jobs > Burst > Synchronous Compilation. In a build it doesn’t matter — there Burst is always compiled ahead of time.

cards.title: All jobs on the main thread
cards.body:
The second question is whether the threads are to blame. Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Use Job Threads: untick it, and every job runs on the main thread right when it’s scheduled. No more parallelism, the order is exactly the order of Schedule(), and breakpoints fire predictably.

The same from code is JobsUtility.JobWorkerCount = 0, and back to automatic is JobsUtility.ResetJobWorkerCount(). After an Editor restart Use Job Threads is on again.

For a single job, Run() is simpler: the same Execute, the same Burst code, but here and now on the current thread.

How to read the result: the bug is gone without threads — so it’s a race or a missing dependency between jobs. With one thread they just happened to run in the “right” order, which nothing guaranteed once threads were involved.

cards.q: A job’s result is sometimes garbage. With Use Job Threads off, the bug never reproduces. Where do you look?
options: For a race or a missing dependency between jobs: without threads they run strictly in Schedule() order
In Burst: it miscompiles the job, so Enable Compilation should stay off for good
For a memory leak: Leak Detection will show where
At FloatMode.Fast: it doesn’t apply with one thread
cards.explain: Use Job Threads removes exactly one thing — parallelism. If the bug is gone without it, two jobs touch the same data with no dependency (or with safety switched off). Find who writes and who reads, and link them with dependsOn.

wrong.1: Burst is the same in both cases; only the parallelism changed.
wrong.2: A leak doesn’t corrupt results — it’s about memory that wasn’t freed.
wrong.3: The float mode is a property of the compiled code; it doesn’t depend on the number of threads.

cards.title: Native debugging of Burst code
cards.body:
If the bug exists only under Burst, you debug the Burst code itself with a native debugger.

Jobs > Burst > Native Debug Mode Compilation turns off optimizations for all Burst code — handy for debugging, but everything gets slower. For one job, use [BurstCompile(Debug = true)]: no optimizations and with debug info; builds respect this flag too. It doesn’t stay in a release.

Then attach a native debugger — Visual Studio, Xcode — to the Editor or to the build, and set breakpoints in the job’s C# source. A build needs symbols: Development Build or Force Debug Information in the Burst AOT settings; they sit next to lib_burst_generated. A breakpoint in code is supported too — System.Diagnostics.Debugger.Break() — but the debugger’s conditional breakpoints are more convenient.

cards.title: Debug.Log in Burst
cards.body:
You can log from Burst, but not the way you do in ordinary C#. Debug.Log, Debug.LogWarning and Debug.LogError take a literal or an interpolated $"..." string (and string.Format with a literal format).

The arguments are built-in value types (int, float, bool, double…) and Unity.Mathematics vectors such as float3. Your own struct’s ToString() won’t work — it prints the type name. You can’t concatenate strings with +, pass a string to your own method or keep it in a field — for text in fields there’s FixedString64Bytes and its relatives.

[BurstDiscard] drops a method from Burst compilation: under Burst the call simply does nothing, and in managed mode the method runs and can touch anything. Such a method can’t return a value.

And a practical point: a log in the Execute of a parallel job over 100,000 elements is 100,000 messages. Log one index, or behind a condition.

cards.q: Which calls compile in a Burst job? Pick all that apply.
options: Debug.Log($"i={i} pos={p}"), where i is an int and p is a float3
Debug.Log("hp: " + hp), where hp is a float
Debug.Log("done")
Debug.Log(name), where name is a string field of the job struct
cards.explain: A literal and an interpolation with primitives and Mathematics vectors are supported. Concatenation with + isn’t: the format has to be a literal. And a string field in a job is impossible in the first place: Burst doesn’t allow strings in struct fields; that’s what FixedString is for.

cards.title: throw and safety checks: Editor vs build
cards.body:
An exception from Burst code is caught in the Editor and printed to the console — the game goes on. In a build, any throw in Burst is an abort: the application crashes. Burst warns about this (BC1370).

That’s why checks with throw go into a method marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")]: such methods and their calls don’t make it into the build. Write the attribute in full — System.Diagnostics.Conditional: a using System.Diagnostics next to UnityEngine makes Debug ambiguous.

Safety checks — out-of-bounds container access, writes to [ReadOnly], races — exist only in the Editor. Jobs > Burst > Enable Safety Checks (Off / On / Force On) controls the checks inside Burst code; Force On turns them on even where DisableSafetyChecks = true is set; after an Editor reload it is On again. The Job System’s own checks are Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Enable Jobs Debugger. In builds these checks are unavailable, not merely switched off — which is why bugs are reproduced in the Editor.

cards.q: The game crashes in a build with no message. In the Editor an exception from a Burst job sometimes shows up in the console, but the game keeps running. What is going on?
options: In the Editor an exception from Burst is caught and logged, while in a build a throw is an abort; find the cause from the Editor exception and wrap the checks in Conditional
Safety checks are off by default in builds — turn them on in Player Settings
Burst ignores throw in builds, so something else is crashing
It’s a memory leak that builds up in the build until it crashes
cards.explain: The same exception looks like a console line in the Editor and like a crash in a build. You look for the cause where it’s visible: in the Editor with Safety Checks. And the checks with throw go into methods marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")], so they stay out of the build.

wrong.1: These checks are unavailable in builds; there is nothing to “turn on” in Player Settings.
wrong.2: The opposite: an unwrapped throw stays in the build and crashes the application.
wrong.3: A leak is shown by Leak Detection, and it doesn’t look like an exception from a job in the Editor console.

cards.title: Leaks: Leak Detection
cards.body:
A native container nobody freed is a leak of unmanaged memory. Leak Detection finds it: Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Leak Detection Level, or NativeLeakDetection.Mode from code.

Enabled (the default in the Editor and development builds) only counts leaks and reports the number at domain unload. Enabled With Stack Trace shows where each unfreed allocation was made — that’s what you want when hunting, but allocations get more expensive, so it’s turned on temporarily. Disabled is the default in regular builds.

The most common cause is an Allocator.Persistent allocation made in Awake with no Dispose() in OnDestroy.

cards.q: A Burst job sometimes gives a wrong result. Put the debugging steps in order.
items: Reproduce in the Editor with Enable Safety Checks and Enable Jobs Debugger
Narrow it down: turn off Use Job Threads, then Enable Compilation
Find the spot: a breakpoint in managed mode, or Debug.Log
If the bug exists only under Burst: Native Debug Mode Compilation and a native debugger
Fix it and check in a build
cards.explain: First give the checks a chance: a safety exception often names the cause right away. Then narrow it down — threads or Burst. Then find the line the cheapest way. The native debugger is for a bug that lives only in Burst code. And check in a build, where there are no checks.

cards.title: Debugging speed: the Profiler and the Burst Inspector
cards.body:
For “too slow” the tools are different. The Profiler’s Timeline view shows jobs on worker threads by name, the main thread’s waits, and how busy the threads are. Inside a job you can mark sections: ProfilerMarker works in Burst — new ProfilerMarker("Name") and Auto() or Begin()/End().

The hot loop is examined in the Burst Inspector: packed or scalar, and what blocked vectorization (lesson 1). Jobs > Burst > Show Timings prints how long each job took to compile.

How to measure honestly: in the Editor, the Jobs Debugger and Safety Checks add their own cost — turn them off for a measurement; Burst must already be compiled (Synchronous Compilation or a warm-up); the final numbers come from a build. For a deep dive into a build, Instruments and Superluminal work with the symbols from lib_burst_generated.

cards.task: Make ApplyDamageJob safe for a build: move the check with throw into static void CheckIndex(int index, int length) marked [System.Diagnostics.Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")], and call it from Execute. Execute itself must have no throw. Rewrite the log with an interpolated $"..." string, without concatenation.

checks.label: CheckIndex is a static void with [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")]
The throw is inside CheckIndex
Execute calls CheckIndex
Execute has no throw
Debug.Log is called with an interpolated $"..."
Debug.Log has no string concatenation with +

cards.explain: In the Editor CheckIndex runs and throws a clear exception that Burst shows in the console. In a build the method and its call are gone, so there is no abort either. String concatenation doesn’t compile in Burst; interpolation with a float does. The attribute is written in full because a using System.Diagnostics next to UnityEngine would make Debug ambiguous.

cards.q: Interviewer: “In the Editor your Burst job is slower than promised. What do you check before drawing conclusions?”
options: That I’m measuring already compiled Burst without extra checks: wait for compilation, turn off the Jobs Debugger and Safety Checks, and take the final measurement in a build
Turn on Native Debug Mode Compilation to see the code more precisely
Add a Debug.Log to Execute to see how many times it runs
Turn off Use Job Threads to remove the threading overhead
cards.explain: In the Editor it’s easy to measure the wrong thing: the first frames of managed code before the background compilation finishes, and safety checks on top of Burst. Remove them or measure in a build, and only then look at the Timeline and the Burst Inspector.

wrong.1: Native Debug Mode turns optimizations off — the code gets even slower, and the measurement means nothing.
wrong.2: A log per element becomes the main workload by itself.
wrong.3: Without worker threads the parallelism is gone — that’s a tool for finding races, not for measuring.

lessons.title: FunctionPointer and SharedStatic
lessons.sub: How to get a “virtual call” and shared statics in Burst, and what they cost

cards.title: Burst has no delegates and no virtual calls
cards.body:
A common question: “How do you do polymorphism in Burst?” First, why the usual route is closed. A virtual call needs a class object, and a delegate is a managed object too. Burst works only with unmanaged data: structs, pointers, native containers.

There are three substitutes, from simple to flexible:

  • a data tag and a switch — few variants, all known;
  • a generic job with an interface constraint — the variant is known at compile time;
  • FunctionPointer<T> — the variant is chosen at runtime, say from a level config.

A senior answer names all three and says what each one costs.

cards.title: FunctionPointer<T>: the declaration
cards.body:
You need four things:

  • a delegate as the “interface” — a plain one, not generic: function pointers do not support generic delegates;
  • [BurstCompile] on the static method and on the type that holds it — otherwise Burst will not find the method;
  • [MonoPInvokeCallback(typeof(Delegate))] from the AOT namespace — for IL2CPP;
  • BurstCompiler.CompileFunctionPointer<T>(Method) — call it once from managed code and keep the result, a FunctionPointer<T>.

Parameters follow the native interop rules: numbers, pointers, ref to them. Structs, float4 included, go only by ref/in/out or by pointer, never by value; return a struct result through out. bool and char are not on the list of allowed types. NativeArray and most native containers cannot be passed: they carry managed safety-system fields.

cards.title: A FunctionPointer in a job is your “virtual call”
cards.body:
FunctionPointer<T> is a struct that holds the address of a compiled function. You can put it in a job field and call it with .Invoke(...). The main thread decides which function to call when it schedules the job: one job, different rules, and nothing to recompile.

For jobs, Burst compiles function pointers asynchronously, just like the jobs themselves.
flow: Update: pick a pointer, put it in a job field

cards.q: Which delegates can be compiled into a FunctionPointer<T>? Select all that apply.
options: delegate float Rule(float d, float v);
delegate void Blend(in float4 a, in float4 b, out float4 r);
delegate float4 Shift(float4 v);
delegate void Sum(NativeArray<float> data);
delegate T Pick<T>(T a, T b);
cards.explain: Numbers by value are fine. float4 is a struct, so only by in/out/ref: the second option is right, the third (float4 by value, and as the return) is not. A NativeArray cannot be passed because of its managed safety fields. Function pointers do not support generic delegates.

cards.title: The cost: an indirect call per element
cards.body:
A call through a pointer jumps to an address the compiler does not know. That costs three things:

  • no inlining — the function body is not merged into the loop;
  • no vectorization across the call — the function gets one scalar at a time, so there is no SIMD over four to eight elements at once;
  • no aliasing information — in a job Burst knows the containers do not overlap ([NoAlias] by default), a function pointer gets none of that.

The Burst docs say it plainly: use a job where you can. If you need a pointer, call it per batch, not per element: pass a pointer to the data and a count, and let the loop live inside the function. In the docs’ example, batches were 1.53× faster than per-element calls, and a plain IJobParallelFor without a pointer was another 1.26× faster than the batches.

cards.q: A job over a million elements calls rule.Invoke(...) for every element and is nearly twice as slow as the same job with the formula written right in Execute. What is the main reason?
options: Every call is indirect: the function cannot be inlined, the loop cannot be vectorized, and there is no aliasing information
Invoke allocates on the heap every time
A FunctionPointer always runs on the main thread
Burst copies the NativeArray on every call
cards.explain: A pointer is a jump to an unknown address. The compiler cannot see the function body, so it can neither inline it nor turn the loop into SIMD. The fix is batching (a pointer to the data plus a count) or a generic job if the rule is known at compile time.

wrong.1: A FunctionPointer is a struct with an address; calling it allocates nothing.
wrong.2: The pointer is called wherever the job runs — on a worker thread.
wrong.3: You cannot pass an array to a function pointer at all; there is no copy, only the cost of the call itself.

cards.title: Static polymorphism: a generic job
cards.body:
If the variant is known at compile time, make the rule a struct that implements an interface, and make the job generic: struct MoveJob<TRule> : IJobParallelFor where TRule : struct, ISpeedRule. Burst compiles a separate version for each concrete type: the call rule.Speed(...) is known up front, so it can be inlined and vectorized together with the loop. Burst supports interface calls through a generic struct constraint.

The condition: a concrete type where you schedule — new MoveJob<Flee>. If the type arrives through a generic parameter, for instance the job is scheduled from a generic method Schedule<T>(), Burst will not find that version in a build: fast in the Editor, slow in the player. Burst does not support scheduling generic jobs through generic methods.

Summary: switch when there are few variants; generic when the type is known at compile time; FunctionPointer when the rule is chosen at runtime — and then in batches.

cards.task: Build a behaviour rule with a FunctionPointer. In the Rules class, write a static method Flee(float distance, float baseSpeed) that returns baseSpeed * 2, with the attributes [BurstCompile] and [MonoPInvokeCallback(typeof(SpeedRule))]. In MoveJob, add a FunctionPointer<Rules.SpeedRule> field and call it in Execute with Invoke(distance[i], baseSpeed). In RuleSetup.Compile, compile Rules.Flee with BurstCompiler.CompileFunctionPointer.

checks.label: The Flee method has [BurstCompile]
The Flee method has [MonoPInvokeCallback(typeof(SpeedRule))]
Flee matches the delegate signature and returns baseSpeed * 2
MoveJob has a FunctionPointer<Rules.SpeedRule> field
Execute calls the rule with .Invoke(distance[i], baseSpeed)
Compile calls BurstCompiler.CompileFunctionPointer<Rules.SpeedRule>(Rules.Flee)

cards.explain: The attribute on the type and on the method lets Burst find the method; MonoPInvokeCallback is for IL2CPP. Compile once from managed code and cache it; the job gets a ready pointer. In the interview, add the cost: the call is indirect, so in a hot loop prefer batches or a generic job.

cards.title: SharedStatic<T>: mutable statics for Burst
cards.body:
Burst can read static readonly fields: it evaluates them and the static constructors at compile time and bakes the values into the code. Burst code cannot write to an ordinary static field, and in a plain C# job statics have no protection at all and can crash the application.

If both C# and Burst code need mutable data, there is SharedStatic<T>: a piece of native memory both sides can see.

  • get it with SharedStatic<T>.GetOrCreate<Context, Key>() — a context type and an empty key class name the field;
  • .Data returns a ref T: read it, write it, take a ref;
  • initialise it from a static constructor in C# before Burst touches it, or the state is undefined.

The cost: it is global state. The safety system does not see it, so it will not catch a race from a parallel job. Write from many threads only atomically, with Interlocked (allowed in Burst). Use it for global flags, settings and debug counters, and pass a job its data through fields and containers.

cards.q: This job is scheduled with Schedule(n, 64), and the counter ends up lower than it should be. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: Data++ means read, add, write. Two worker threads read the same value, and one of the increments is lost. The safety system cannot see this race: a SharedStatic is not a native container. Use Interlocked.Increment(ref Stats.Hits.Data) or, better, count per thread and add up after the job.

cards.q: Match the task to the tool.
pairs: The rule comes from the level config at runtime
Three behaviours, known at compile time, a hot loop
a generic job with where T : struct, an interface
A counter that both C# and Burst code read and write
A table of constants that never changes

cards.q: Interviewer: “How do you make a virtual call in Burst?” Which answer is stronger?
options: Burst has no delegates or virtual calls — those are managed objects. If the variant is known at compile time, I use a generic job with a struct rule: Burst instantiates it and the call can be inlined. If it is chosen at runtime, I use a FunctionPointer<T> from CompileFunctionPointer, but the call is indirect, with no inlining or vectorization, so I call it on a batch of data
I put objects implementing an interface into a NativeArray and call the interface method in Execute
I use a FunctionPointer<T>: Burst inlines it, so it costs the same as a normal call
You can’t; Burst only has a switch over an enum
cards.explain: A strong answer names the mechanism (why it is not allowed), the two working routes and their cost. That is what marks a senior: not “there is FunctionPointer”, but when you need it and how not to lose speed on it.

wrong.1: You cannot put a class object into a NativeArray: the container holds only unmanaged structs.
wrong.2: A call through a pointer is indirect: the compiler does not know the address and cannot inline the function.
wrong.3: A switch is only the simplest route; a generic job and FunctionPointer work too.

lessons.title: Transforms and physics from jobs
lessons.sub: TransformAccessArray, IJobParallelForTransform and batched physics queries instead of thousands of calls

cards.title: Unity objects are not allowed in jobs
cards.body:
GameObject, Transform, GetComponent, Physics.Raycast, Time.time are main-thread API, and engine objects are managed. You cannot touch them in a job, let alone in Burst code.

Yet the most common bulk operations in a game are moving transforms and casting rays. For these Unity offers two official ways out:

  • TransformAccessArray + IJobParallelForTransform — reading and writing transforms on worker threads;
  • batched physics queries — RaycastCommand and its relatives: thousands of queries in one call, executed in jobs.

This is the built-in physics (PhysX, the UnityEngine.PhysicsModule module), not the Unity Physics package for Entities.

cards.title: TransformAccessArray and IJobParallelForTransform
cards.body:
TransformAccessArray is a native list of transforms. Create it once from an array (new TransformAccessArray(transforms)) or grow it with Add and RemoveAtSwapBack. It is native memory, so Dispose() is mandatory.

An IJobParallelForTransform job gets Execute(int index, TransformAccess transform). TransformAccess has position, rotation, localPosition, localRotation, localScale, the matrices, SetPositionAndRotation and isValid. The index matches the index in the array — use it to read your own data from a NativeArray.

Anything you need from main-thread API (time, input) you compute up front and pass in a field. Schedule with Schedule(transforms) in Update, complete in LateUpdate, and in OnDestroy call Complete() first, then Dispose().

cards.title: The trap: only different roots run in parallel
cards.body:
The writing Schedule(transforms) parallelizes work across different hierarchies. Transforms that share a root object are always processed on the same thread: Unity does not let two threads write into one hierarchy.
