So 10 000 enemies parented under one Enemies object “to keep the hierarchy tidy” will run on a single thread. You get Burst, but no parallelism. The fix is to keep objects that move in bulk at the scene root, or to split them across several roots.

If you only need to read — gather positions for another job — there is ScheduleReadOnly(transforms, batchSize): it reads all transforms in parallel regardless of the hierarchy. A transform may have been destroyed there, so check isValid. For debugging there is RunReadOnly; this job has no plain Run.

cards.q: 10 000 enemies are children of one Enemies object. An IJobParallelForTransform with [BurstCompile] moves them via Schedule(transforms), and the Profiler Timeline shows the job on a single worker thread. Why?
options: All the transforms share a root, and the writing Schedule only parallelizes different hierarchies
JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() was not called
IJobParallelForTransform always runs on one thread
Burst cannot vectorize TransformAccess
cards.explain: Transforms with a shared root are processed by one thread. Move the enemies to the scene root or split them across several roots, and the work spreads over the workers. If you only read, ScheduleReadOnly parallelizes regardless of the hierarchy.

wrong.1: Without ScheduleBatchedJobs the job starts later, but it is still handed out to the workers.
wrong.2: With different roots the work is split across the worker threads.
wrong.3: Vectorization is about instructions within a thread; it has nothing to do with the thread count.

cards.q: What can you do inside Execute(int i, TransformAccess t) of an IJobParallelForTransform? Select all that apply.
options: Write t.localPosition
Read Time.deltaTime
Call t.SetPositionAndRotation(p, r)
Get GetComponent<Rigidbody>() of this object
Read a speed from a [ReadOnly] NativeArray at index i
cards.explain: TransformAccess gives position, rotation, scale and SetPositionAndRotation, and the job reads its own data from native containers by index. Time and GetComponent are main-thread API: time is passed in a field, and components are not reachable from a job.

cards.title: RaycastCommand: hundreds of rays in one call
cards.body:
Instead of a loop of Physics.Raycast, build a batch:

  • a NativeArray<RaycastCommand> — one command per ray: new RaycastCommand(from, direction, queryParameters, distance);
  • a NativeArray<RaycastHit> of size commands × maxHits;
  • RaycastCommand.ScheduleBatch(commands, results, minCommandsPerJob, maxHits, dependsOn) — it returns a JobHandle.

The rays run in jobs, in parallel with each other. minCommandsPerJob is the minimum number of commands per job, much like batchSize. Until Complete() is called, results is off-limits.

QueryParameters (since 2022.2) sets the layer mask, triggers, back faces and multiple hits per mesh; there is QueryParameters.Default. The old constructors taking layerMask and maxHits are deprecated: maxHits now goes to ScheduleBatch, and without it it is 1.

cards.title: Reading the results and building a chain
cards.body:
The results of command N start at index N × maxHits. If there are fewer hits than maxHits, the first empty result is marked by collider == null — stop there. The command does not overwrite the slots after it, so they may hold garbage from last time.

hit.collider is a managed object, so you read it on the main thread. The numbers — point, normal, distance — can be processed in a following job too.

You can fill the commands in a Burst job and pass its JobHandle as dependsOn — that gives a chain with no Complete() in the middle. If you cast rays every frame, do not reallocate the buffers: create them once with Allocator.Persistent in Awake and free them in OnDestroy. In the Profiler the batch shows up as BatchQuery.ExecuteRaycastJob.

SpherecastCommand, BoxcastCommand, CapsulecastCommand, ClosestPointCommand (since 2022.1) and OverlapSphereCommand, OverlapBoxCommand, OverlapCapsuleCommand (since 2022.2, results are ColliderHit) work the same way.

cards.q: Put one frame with a batch of rays in order.
items: Allocate a NativeArray<RaycastCommand> and a NativeArray<RaycastHit> of commands × maxHits
Fill the commands: new RaycastCommand(from, direction, query, distance)
RaycastCommand.ScheduleBatch(commands, results, 32, maxHits) and ScheduleBatchedJobs()
The main thread does its own work while the rays run in jobs
Complete() and read the results up to the first collider == null
Dispose() the temporary arrays
cards.explain: Buffers and commands first, then one call to schedule the batch. While the rays fly, the main thread is free. Read the results only after Complete(), and free the memory only after that.

cards.task: Replace the 500 Physics.Raycast calls in GroundProbe with one batch. In Update, fill commands with new RaycastCommand(..., QueryParameters, 10f) and schedule RaycastCommand.ScheduleBatch(commands, results, 32, 1), keeping the JobHandle in a field. In LateUpdate, call Complete() and update groundY only where collider != null. In OnDestroy, wait for the batch before Dispose().

checks.label: The JobHandle is a field, and Update assigns it RaycastCommand.ScheduleBatch(commands, results, ...)
Update fills the commands with new RaycastCommand using QueryParameters
No Physics.Raycast is left
Update has no Complete()
LateUpdate calls Complete() first, then checks collider != null
In OnDestroy, Complete() comes before Dispose()

cards.explain: The 500 rays go out as one batch and run on worker threads while the rest of the frame executes. The buffers are Persistent, allocated once. Without Complete() in OnDestroy, the batch could write into results after Dispose(). To take the filling off the main thread too, build the commands in a Burst job and pass its JobHandle to ScheduleBatch.

cards.q: 100 commands, maxHits = 4. Where do the results of the command at index 7 live, and how far do you read?
options: From index 28; read up to the first result with collider == null, but no further than 31
From index 7; all commands’ results are laid out back to back
From index 28; read all four, the empty slots are zeroed
From index 700; each command gets 100 slots
cards.explain: Command N starts at N × maxHits = 28 and occupies slots 28–31. The first empty slot is marked with collider == null, and the command does not overwrite the ones after it — old contents may remain there.

wrong.1: Each command gets maxHits slots, so it starts at N × maxHits.
wrong.2: Only the first empty slot is cleared; beyond it there are no guarantees.
wrong.3: The array size is commands × maxHits, i.e. 400 slots for all commands.

cards.q: You need 2000 “who is inside the blast radius” checks per frame. What do you use?
options: OverlapSphereCommand.ScheduleBatch: a batch of queries in jobs, results are ColliderHit
Physics.OverlapSphere inside an IJobParallelFor
360 RaycastCommands in every direction from each point
An IJobParallelForTransform over every object in the scene
cards.explain: Overlaps have their own batches: OverlapSphereCommand, OverlapBoxCommand, OverlapCapsuleCommand (since 2022.2). They work like RaycastCommand: an array of commands, an array of results, ScheduleBatch and a JobHandle.

wrong.1: Physics.* is main-thread API; you cannot call it in a job.
wrong.2: Rays give an approximation and hundreds of times more queries than needed.
wrong.3: That job moves and reads transforms; it does not run physics queries.

cards.q: Interviewer: “How do you move 10 000 ordinary GameObjects from jobs?” Which answer is stronger?
options: One manager instead of 10 000 Updates: a TransformAccessArray created once and a Burst IJobParallelForTransform. I pass time and input in fields, Schedule in Update, Complete in LateUpdate, Dispose in OnDestroy. I keep the objects under different roots: transforms with a shared root go on one thread
I grab each object’s transform right inside an IJobParallelFor
With Parallel.For over a Transform array
I move everything to Entities — there is no other way
cards.explain: A strong answer covers the tool, the buffer’s lifetime and the main hierarchy trap. If the interviewer asks “why one thread?”, you have already answered it.

wrong.1: Transform is a managed main-thread object; an ordinary job cannot touch it.
wrong.2: Transform API may be called only from the main thread; Parallel.For does not change that.
wrong.3: Entities is an option, but TransformAccessArray solves this with GameObjects too.

lessons.title: When you don’t need Burst
lessons.sub: Small data, branchy logic, managed dependencies, maintainability — and why the profiler comes first

cards.title: Jobs and Burst have a cost
cards.body:
What marks a senior is not having rewritten everything in Burst, but knowing where it pays off. The cost has three parts:

  • scheduling — copying the job struct, the queue, waking threads, Complete(); in the Editor, safety system checks on top;
  • moving data — if the data lives in objects, every frame it is gathered into a NativeArray and scattered back, and the main thread does that;
  • code — the HPC# subset, a second data model, manual Dispose(), harder debugging.

Burst wins big on tight loops over arrays of numbers. If gathering and scattering around such a loop take longer than the loop itself, those are what you speed up — for example with a TransformAccessArray, or by keeping the data in native arrays permanently.

cards.title: Small data
cards.body:
With a dozen elements the work is cheaper than queueing it. There is no magic threshold — only a measurement gives you one — but the options are known:

  • plain C# — often the right answer: simpler and no slower;
  • the same Burst job via Run() — Burst code, but no queue and no threads;
  • a static [BurstCompile] method called directly — Burst without jobs; parameters follow the native call rules: numbers and pointers, structs by ref/in, no generics and no NativeArray.

Jobs on several threads pay off when there is a lot of work and the main thread is busy with its own in the meantime.

cards.q: An inventory has 16 slots, and every frame each one gets its tooltip recomputed. A colleague suggests an IJobParallelFor with [BurstCompile]. What do you say?
options: Keep plain C#: 16 elements are cheaper to compute than to queue — and first check in the Profiler that it even shows up
Agree: Burst speeds up any code
Use an IJobParallelFor with batchSize = 1 so each slot gets its own thread
Move the computation into a SharedStatic to avoid copying data
cards.explain: At 16 elements scheduling costs more than the work, and tooltips usually pull in strings and UI that Burst does not have. If the Profiler shows it is a hot spot, first ask why it is recomputed every frame.

wrong.1: Burst speeds up numeric loops over unmanaged data; it does not remove scheduling overhead.
wrong.2: 16 tiny batches mean paying for work stealing 16 times and getting almost nothing.
wrong.3: A SharedStatic is a shared static; it has nothing to do with how fast the computation runs.

cards.title: Branches and managed dependencies
cards.body:
Burst gives the most where data is contiguous, branches are few and the loop can be turned into SIMD. It gives less where there are:

  • lots of branches — each iteration takes its own path, there is nothing to vectorize;
  • traversal by reference — trees and graphs of objects: the time goes into cache misses, not computation;
  • managed dependencies — strings, events, UI, LINQ, GetComponent, FindObjectsByType every frame: that code cannot move into Burst, and moving the data costs more than you would gain.

The rule: move the numeric core into Burst, not the whole system. Decision logic stays in ordinary C#; heavy math over arrays goes into a job.

cards.q: What is worth moving into a Burst job first? Select all that apply.
options: Updating 50 000 particle positions every frame
Testing 20 000 points against the camera frustum
Parsing a JSON config when a level loads
Dialogue logic with strings and UI events
Generating a 1024×1024 height map from noise
cards.explain: Particles, the frustum and noise are tight numeric loops over arrays: exactly what Burst is for. JSON is parsed once at load time and is all strings. Dialogue is branches, strings and UI, with managed dependencies on every line.

cards.title: Maintainability is a cost too
cards.body:
Burst code lives by its own rules: unmanaged data only, containers with manual Dispose(), a second copy of the state next to the objects, debugging by turning Burst off or with a native debugger. Everyone who touches the system has to know all that.

To keep the cost reasonable:

  • a thin shell outside, a Burst core inside — the rest of the game sees an ordinary C# API;
  • one owner for the buffers — whoever allocates them frees them;
  • the core is pure math with no Unity API: with Burst off, the same code runs as ordinary C#, and it is easy to cover with a test.

If the gain is a fraction of a millisecond in a non-critical system, the honest call is not to rewrite it.

cards.title: Profiler first
cards.body:
“Profile first, then Burst the hot loop.” The order is:

  • measure in a Development Build on the target device: in the Editor, safety checks and the Jobs Debugger are on, Burst compiles asynchronously so the first frames run managed code, and the Editor adds its own overhead. Deep Profile helps you search, but it distorts timings;
  • find where the frame goes: main thread, render thread or GPU, GC.Alloc, waiting for jobs (WaitForJobGroupID on the main thread). Burst only speeds up CPU computation;
  • estimate the ceiling: if a method takes 1 ms of 16, even an infinite speed-up saves 1 ms;
  • add your own markers and compare “before” and “after” on the same scenario.

A marker is a ProfilerMarker from Unity.Profiling. Create it once in a static readonly field and wrap the section in using (marker.Auto()) or a Begin()/End() pair. It does not allocate, shows up in the Profiler’s Hierarchy and Timeline, and works in Burst code. A Stopwatch with Debug.Log every frame is expensive in itself: a string, a log write, a stack trace — and ends up measuring itself.

cards.q: A frame takes 20 ms, and the AI method takes 2 ms of it. You rewrote the method in Burst and made it 10× faster. How long is the frame now?
options: About 18.2 ms: the method takes 0.2 ms, 1.8 ms saved
About 2 ms: everything got 10× faster
About 10 ms
About 19.8 ms
cards.explain: Only the method itself gets faster: 20 − 2 + 0.2 = 18.2 ms. The other 18 ms stay as they were. That is why the profiler comes first: it shows which part of the frame is worth the effort.

cards.q: Profiler: Update takes 3 ms, and the Burst SteerJob takes 0.1 ms of it. Which line is the first candidate to fix?
cards.explain: FindObjectsByType searches the whole scene every frame and allocates a new array. The Burst job is already fast; what is expensive is everything around it: the search and the shuffling through transform. Keep the enemy list in a field and drive the transforms through a TransformAccessArray.

cards.task: Replace the Stopwatch and Debug.Log timing in Crowd with a profiler marker. Declare a static readonly ProfilerMarker named "Crowd.Steer" and wrap the SteerAll() call in Update in using (marker.Auto()). Add using Unity.Profiling; and remove Stopwatch and Debug.Log.

checks.label: The Unity.Profiling namespace is imported
There is a static readonly ProfilerMarker named "Crowd.Steer"
In Update, the SteerAll() call is wrapped in using (marker.Auto())
The marker is not created anew in Update
No Stopwatch and no Debug.Log

cards.explain: The marker is created once; Auto() returns a struct that calls End() when the using block exits — no allocations. The Profiler gets a Crowd.Steer row with exact timing every frame, so “before” and “after” compare fairly. You can place the same markers inside Burst code.

cards.q: Put the work on a “slow” system in order.
items: Make a Development Build and run it on the target device
In the Profiler, find where the frame goes: CPU or GPU, which thread, which methods
Put a ProfilerMarker on the suspect sections and record the “before” time
Move the hot numeric loop into a Burst job
Measure the same scenario again and compare with “before”
cards.explain: First an honest measurement where the game will actually run, then finding the hot spot, then one change, then measuring again. Without “before” there is nothing to compare, and without the profiler it is easy to speed up something that was not worth the time.

cards.q: Interviewer: “Why didn’t you move the whole project to Burst?” Which answer is stronger?
options: Burst pays off on tight numeric loops over arrays. I profile a build first, find the hot spot and move its numeric core into Burst. Small data, branchy logic, strings and UI stay in C#: there the gain is smaller than the cost of scheduling, moving data and maintenance
Burst does not work on mobile platforms
Burst code is slower than plain C# below a thousand iterations
We ran out of time: everything should be moved, it just takes long
cards.explain: A strong answer gives the criterion (where Burst pays off), the process (profiler first) and the cost (scheduling, data, maintenance). It shows you made an engineering decision rather than following a fashion.

wrong.1: Burst compiles for mobile architectures too, including Arm with Neon.
wrong.2: There is no thousand-iteration threshold; there is a scheduling cost, and a measurement shows it.
wrong.3: Moving everything is exactly the mistake: some code only gets more complex, not faster.

lessons.title: Section final: how Burst makes code fast
lessons.sub: Vectorization, data layout, determinism, debugging, polymorphism, transforms and physics — and when you need none of it

cards.title: The section on one screen
cards.body:
No new theory here — just what the questions will need.

  • Vectorization. Burst turns a tight loop into SIMD: one instruction for several floats at once. Branches get in the way (replace if with math.select), and so does aliasing (job containers are [NoAlias] by default). You check it in the Burst Inspector: packed mulps/vmulps instead of scalar mulss.
  • SoA vs AoS. Memory is read in cache lines. With AoS the line also carries fields the loop never touches; with SoA it holds only the values you need, back to back. That is why Entities stores components in chunks by type.
  • Determinism. FloatMode: Default = Strict; Fast reorders operations and may use FMA; Deterministic — since Burst 1.8.25, only on 64-bit architectures and only for Burst code. FloatPrecision sets the accuracy of math functions. Lockstep across platforms often uses fixed-point.
  • Debugging. Jobs > Burst > Enable Compilation turns Burst off so the ordinary debugger works; Enable Safety Checks controls the checks inside Burst code; Native Debug Mode Compilation or [BurstCompile(Debug = true)] is for a native debugger. Debug.Log in Burst takes a literal or $"..." with primitives and Mathematics vectors; a struct’s ToString() does not work.
  • Polymorphism and statics. A generic job with a struct rule when the type is known at compile time; FunctionPointer<T> when it is chosen at runtime, in batches; SharedStatic<T> for shared mutable statics, written atomically.
  • Engine objects. TransformAccessArray + IJobParallelForTransform (only different roots run in parallel), RaycastCommand and the other query batches.
  • When you don’t need it. Small data, branchy logic, managed dependencies. Profiler in a build first.

cards.q: In the Burst Inspector, the ClampJob loop is made of scalar mulss. What do you do first?
options: Remove the branch: r[i] = math.select(0f, v[i] * k, v[i] > 0f), and check in the Inspector that the multiplies are now packed
Put [NoAlias] on v and r
Lower batchSize to 1
Turn on FloatMode.Deterministic
cards.explain: math.select computes both values and picks one without a jump — every element takes the same path, and the loop can become SIMD. After the change, look in the Inspector for mulps or vmulps instead of mulss.

wrong.1: Native containers in job fields are already treated as [NoAlias]; the branch is the problem.
wrong.2: batchSize affects how iterations are handed to threads, not the instructions inside the loop.
wrong.3: Deterministic is about identical results across platforms, not about vectorization.

cards.q: Explain out loud why SoA is faster than AoS. Put the steps of the answer in order.
items: The CPU reads memory not byte by byte but in cache lines, usually 64 bytes
With AoS the line carries the whole struct, including fields the loop never touches
With SoA the line holds only the values the loop reads, back to back
Burst loads contiguous values with one SIMD instruction — the loop vectorizes
cards.explain: Mechanism (cache lines) → what AoS wastes → what SoA gains → why it also means vectorization. That is the order to say it in an interview, finishing with: “and I check it in the Burst Inspector”.

cards.q: What is true about float determinism in Burst? Select all that apply.
options: FloatMode.Deterministic is supported since Burst 1.8.25 and only on 64-bit architectures
FloatMode.Fast may reorder operations and use FMA, so the result can differ from Strict
FloatPrecision.High guarantees identical results on every platform
FloatMode.Deterministic also makes the ordinary C# code around the job deterministic
Lockstep across different platforms often uses fixed-point instead of float
cards.explain: Deterministic arrived in 1.8.25 and works only on 64-bit architectures and only for Burst code: non-deterministic inputs from outside break it. Fast trades accuracy for speed. FloatPrecision is about the accuracy of functions like sin and exp, not about matching across platforms.

cards.q: Interviewer: “A job gives wrong results with Burst and correct ones with Burst off. How do you track it down?” Which answer is stronger?
options: I make sure Jobs > Burst > Enable Safety Checks is on, so Burst code catches out-of-bounds access. I look at FloatMode: Fast reorders operations. Then Debug.Log with primitives inside the Burst code, or [BurstCompile(Debug = true)] and a native debugger
I call Debug.Log(ToString()) on the job struct inside Execute and compare the output
Burst cannot be debugged, so I rewrite the job without Burst
I set a breakpoint in Execute and inspect the Burst code’s values in the ordinary debugger
cards.explain: A Burst vs non-Burst difference is most often checks that were switched off, or the order of float operations. Cheap steps come first, the native debugger last.

wrong.1: A struct’s ToString() does not work in Burst — it prints the type name. Log a literal or $"..." with primitives.
wrong.2: It can be debugged: by turning compilation off, with Debug.Log, with a native debugger and Debug = true.
wrong.3: With a managed debugger attached, Burst is turned off for that code path — you would see the managed version, which is exactly the one that works.

cards.q: A hot loop over a million elements has three movement rules, all known at compile time. Right now a FunctionPointer is called per element. What do you suggest?
options: A generic MoveJob<TRule> with struct rules: Burst compiles a version per rule, the call can be inlined and the loop vectorized
Keep the FunctionPointer: Burst inlines it like a normal call
Put a Func<float, float, float> delegate in a job field
Make the rules subclasses of a base class with a virtual method
cards.explain: If the type is known at compile time, you do not need an indirect call. The key is to schedule a concrete type (new MoveJob<Flee>), not through a generic method, or Burst will not find the version in a build.

wrong.1: A call through a pointer is indirect — it cannot be inlined.
wrong.2: A delegate is a managed object; Burst does not have them.
wrong.3: A virtual call needs a class object — managed again.

cards.q: A trap. maxHits = 4, and sometimes objects the ray never hit take damage. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: The first empty result is marked with collider == null, and the command does not overwrite the slots after it: hits from previous frames stay there. It needs break, not continue — the first empty result ends that command’s results.

cards.task: Replace the FunctionPointer in MoveJob with static polymorphism. Make the job generic: struct MoveJob<TRule> : IJobParallelFor where TRule : struct, ISpeedRule, with a field of type TRule; in Execute call rule.Speed(distance[i], baseSpeed). In Steering.Schedule, schedule new MoveJob<Flee> with Schedule(distance.Length, 64) and return the JobHandle. Do not make Schedule itself a generic method.

checks.label: MoveJob is declared as MoveJob<T> : IJobParallelFor where T : struct, ISpeedRule
MoveJob has a field of the type parameter
Execute calls .Speed(distance[i], baseSpeed)
FunctionPointer is no longer used
A concrete type is scheduled: new MoveJob<Flee> … .Schedule(
Steering.Schedule is not a generic method

cards.explain: The rule type is known at compile time, so Burst builds MoveJob<Flee> separately, and the Speed call is an ordinary direct call that can be inlined. A concrete type at the scheduling site lets Burst find that version in a build too. Keep FunctionPointer for rules chosen at runtime.

cards.q: You moved the AI system into a Burst job. The Profiler shows the job at 0.1 ms, but the frame barely changed. What is most likely?
options: The expensive part was not the computation but what surrounds it: gathering data from objects and scattering it back, or another part of the frame entirely — the hot spot had to be found with the profiler first
Burst did not kick in, and without it the job does not run
batchSize has to go down to 1
The Profiler does not show the time of Burst jobs
cards.explain: Only what you sped up gets faster: if the computation was a small part of the frame, the frame barely moves. Markers and a measurement first, then move into Burst what is actually expensive.

wrong.1: Without Burst the job still runs — as ordinary C#, only slower.
wrong.2: batchSize changes how iterations are handed out; the job is already 0.1 ms.
wrong.3: Burst jobs show up in the Timeline on worker threads like any other job.

cards.task: Replace 10 000 Spinner components with one SpinManager. In Awake, create a TransformAccessArray from items. Finish SpinJob: Execute(int index, TransformAccess transform) rotates localRotation by delta. In Update, compute delta on the main thread (Time.deltaTime only here), schedule new SpinJob { ... }.Schedule(transforms) and keep the JobHandle in a field. In LateUpdate call Complete(); in OnDestroy call Complete() and then transforms.Dispose().

checks.label: Awake creates new TransformAccessArray(items)
Execute(int, TransformAccess) writes the transform’s rotation
The JobHandle is a field, and Update assigns it new SpinJob { ... }.Schedule(transforms)
SpinJob does not touch Time
LateUpdate calls Complete()
OnDestroy calls Complete() first, then transforms.Dispose()

cards.explain: 10 000 Update calls become one Burst job on worker threads. Time is main-thread API, so the per-frame rotation is computed in Update and passed in a field. The objects sit at the scene root — otherwise the writing Schedule would hand them all to one thread. Without Complete() in OnDestroy, Dispose() could free the array under a running job.

cards.title: Practice in Unity: 10 000 cubes and a batch of rays
cards.body:
Setup (Unity 6, the Burst, Collections and Mathematics packages, 40–60 minutes). A scene with a ground plane and a spawner that creates 10 000 cubes at the scene root; each has a Spinner component that rotates it in its own Update. Make a Development Build.

  1. Measure “before”. In the Profiler (CPU Usage, Timeline view), note the main-thread BehaviourUpdate time per frame.
  2. TransformAccessArray. Remove Spinner and hook up the SpinManager from the task above. In the Timeline, SpinJob should run on several worker threads, and the main thread should spend only the scheduling and Complete() on rotation.
  3. The hierarchy trap. Parent all the cubes under one object and measure again: the job drops to one thread. Move the cubes back to the root.
  4. A batch of rays. Add 500 agents and a GroundProbe with RaycastCommand; compare it with the Physics.Raycast version. The batch shows up as BatchQuery.ExecuteRaycastJob on worker threads. Wrap both versions in a ProfilerMarker.
  5. Burst Inspector. Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector: compare the MoveJob with a FunctionPointer and MoveJob<Flee>. The first has a call through an address in a register or memory inside the loop; the second has no call. Turn on Highlight SIMD Scalar vs Packed and see whether the multiplies are packed.

It worked if the main-thread rotation time dropped several times over, SpinJob is spread across worker threads, the one-root experiment showed the difference, the rays left the main thread, and you have written down the “before” and “after” numbers in milliseconds. Those numbers are what you tell in the interview: what you did, what you got, and why you stopped there.
